relations.note: Aditi is the mother of the divine Āditya group.

relations.myth: Aditi presents seven sons to the gods
relations.note: Aditi approaches the gods accompanied by seven of her eight sons.

relations.myth: Seven accepted sons and rejected Mārtāṇḍa
relations.note: Aditi presents seven Ādityas, rejects Mārtāṇḍa, then restores him to mortality.
Aditi is invoked with Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa for divine favor.
Aditi helps prompt the consecration in which Airāvata transports heavenly water.
Aditi and Aryaman are invoked within the protective Āditya group.
Aryaman is one of Aditi's principal Vedic sons.
Bali dispossesses Aditi's sons; her vow enables Vāmana to recover their worlds.
Aditi’s austerity and request bring about Vāmana’s incarnation against Bali.
Aditi is associated with Bhaga in the protective Āditya collective.
Bhaga is counted among Aditi's Āditya sons.
Some Purāṇas derive Dakṣa from Brahmā, making Aditi Brahmā's later descendant.

relations.myth: Reciprocal generation of Aditi and Dakṣa
relations.note: Aditi is born from Dakṣa in the same circular cosmogony.
Epic and Purāṇic genealogies conventionally make Aditi Dakṣa's daughter.
Aditi is born from Daksha in the same reciprocal creation.

relations.myth: Reciprocal generation of Aditi and Dakṣa
relations.note: Dakṣa is born from Aditi in the Vedic cosmogony.
Daksha is named among Aditi’s Āditya circle.
Daksha is born from Aditi in a reciprocal creation paradox.

relations.myth: Aditi identified with all cosmic relations
relations.note: Aditi is poetically identified with sky, atmosphere, mother, father, and son.
Later Vedic, epic, and Purāṇic traditions make Indra Aditi's son.
Aditi performs a vow enabling Viṣṇu to restore dispossessed Indra.
Later readings say Aditi and the divine mothers direct Surabhi’s consecration of Kṛṣṇa.
Aditi attends Skanda's consecration among gods and divine mothers.
As Diti’s sister and Indra’s mother, Aditi is the Maruts’ aunt in later genealogy.
Aditi, Mitra, and Varuṇa jointly receive prayers for favor and protection.
Mitra belongs to the principal Vedic Ādityas born from Aditi.
Some passages make Aditi cosmically coextensive with Heaven and Earth, but inconsistently.

relations.myth: Cosmic invocations with Heaven and Earth
relations.note: Aditi appears beside Heaven and Earth in several cosmic invocations.
Later genealogies classify Pūṣan as an Āditya and son of Aditi.
Aditi is mother of the Rudras with Kaśyapa in some genealogies.
Later classifications include Savitṛ among Aditi's twelve Āditya sons.
Later Vedic and epic-Purāṇic traditions include the solar deity among Aditi's offspring.
Aditi bears Sūrya as Mārtaṇḍa among her eight sons.
Some post-Vedic Āditya lists make Tvaṣṭṛ a son of Aditi.
Aditi bears Viṣṇu's dwarf incarnation Vāmana.
Vāmana recovers the worlds from Bali and restores Aditi's sons.
Aditi and Varuṇa are jointly invoked to release worshippers from bonds and guilt.
Varuṇa is one of Aditi's principal Vedic Āditya sons.
Alternative creation catalogues place the Vasus among Aditi's divine offspring.
Aditi appears beside the Vasus in early divine classifications.

relations.myth: Viṣṇu promises incarnation as her son
relations.note: Viṣṇu answers Aditi's devotion by promising to enter Kaśyapa and become her son.

Aditi worships Viṣṇu through austerity and a milk-centered vow.
Agni serves as their mouth and tongue, carrying sacrificial offerings.
Agni acts as messenger during their ritual rivalry with the Aṅgirases.

relations.myth: The gods grant a thornless path
relations.note: Aryaman joins the collective in granting worshippers safe passage.
After Bali displaces the gods, their brother Vāmana recovers divine sovereignty.
Bhaga is invoked within the collective as distributor of shares and fortune.
Purāṇic cosmology places Brahmā as progenitor above Kaśyapa and the Ādityas.

The seven Ādityas protect Soma and the worshipper.

relations.myth: Aditi and Dakṣa mutually generate one another
relations.note: Dakṣa participates in reciprocal cosmogony with the Ādityas’ mother and belongs to their early group.

relations.myth: Indra joins and leads the Ādityas
relations.note: Indra enters later enumerations and becomes leader of the group in epic genealogy.

relations.myth: Ādityas invoked through Manu’s first sacrifice
relations.note: The Ādityas are asked to grant the safety associated with Manu’s primordial sacrifice.

relations.myth: Divine hosts in the solar hierarchy
relations.note: The Maruts appear beside the Ādityas in hymns and solar cosmology.

Later lists classify Savitr as one of twelve Ādityas.

Viṣṇu incarnates as Vāmana and recovers the worlds for Aditi’s sons.

relations.myth: Ādityas consume the sun’s third nectar

One hymn addresses or characterizes the Ādityas themselves as Vasus.

relations.myth: Assembly of the gods in heaven

relations.myth: Viṣṇu becomes foremost among the twelve

relations.note: Agni and Vāyu are coordinated as terrestrial and atmospheric cosmic powers.

Airāvata is listed among Vāsuki’s brothers or close serpent kin.
Viṣṇu participates in the churning from which Airāvata emerges.
Vṛtrāsura engulfs Airāvata together with Indra during their battle.

Brahmā restores Andhaka’s sight and grants qualified invulnerability.

Brahmā restores Andhaka’s sight and grants a boon conditioned by maternal desire.

relations.myth: Birth complex of Vasiṣṭha and Agastya
relations.note: Seeing Urvaśī causes Mitra’s emission, contributing to an extraordinary vessel-birth tradition.

relations.note: Urvaśī participates with Varuṇa in the emission and vessel-birth complex.
Apsarases emerge during the ocean churning that Viṣṇu directs or enables.

Śeṣa supports or attends Varāha, whose foot rests upon his jeweled hood.
Varuṇa sends Vāruṇī and her divine liquor for Balarāma’s enjoyment.
Varuṇa welcomes and worships the serpent issuing from Balarāma at death.
Ananta assists Vāsuki by repeatedly raising and lowering his hood.
Later visual and sectarian systems sometimes merge Vāsuki with Śeṣa.

relations.myth: Nāgas receive Balarāma’s returning serpent essence
relations.note: Vāsuki receives the thousand-headed serpent emerging from Balarāma at death.
Vāsuki is one of Śeṣa’s named nāga brothers.
Vaiṣṇava systems classify Śeṣa as Viṣṇu’s power, manifestation, or expansion.

relations.myth: Viṣṇu reclines upon Śeṣa during cosmic suspension
relations.note: Śeṣa forms Viṣṇu’s couch and canopy upon the cosmic ocean.
Śeṣa-Ananta serves as Vishnu’s serpent couch upon the causal ocean.

relations.myth: Yamunā submits and gives Balarāma gifts
relations.note: After submitting to Balarāma, Yamunā presents him with gifts.
Balarāma drags Yamunā with his plough until she submits to his summons.
Śiva and Viṣṇu jointly battle demons in accommodative sectarian narratives.
Viṣṇu seeks the fiery pillar’s lower limit and admits failure.
Harihara imagery fuses Śiva and Viṣṇu into one composite deity.
Śukra and Sūrya appear jointly in Navagraha ritual and iconography.
Śukra recognizes Vāmana as Viṣṇu and advises Bali to refuse him.
Śukra recognizes Vāmana, warns Bali, and attempts to obstruct the gift.
Vāmana pierces the vessel spout with kuśa grass, injuring Śukra’s eye.
Vāmana clears the vessel spout with kuśa grass and blinds Śukra in one eye.
Viṣṇu kills Śukra’s mother while she protects Asuras; Śukra’s direct action varies.
The brothers appropriate Sūrya’s solar office.
The brothers appropriate Varuṇa’s cosmic authority.
The brothers appropriate Vāyu’s power or splendor.
As Lakṣmī, Sītā accompanies Viṣṇu in his incarnation as Rāma.
As Rāma, Vishnu wages war against Rāvaṇa and recovers the abducted Sītā.
Sītā bows, petitions Yamuna, and promises substantial offerings after Rāma's safe return.
Later imagery conflates Uchchaihshravas with Sūrya’s horses, partly through Revanta’s solar parentage.
Uṣas precedes Sūrya and opens the road for his appearance.
Sūrya follows Uṣas like a young man pursuing a maiden.
Sūrya transmits or pronounces the Gāyatrī for Vāmana.
Sūrya is Varuṇa’s eye; Varuṇa helps regulate his celestial course.
Varuṇa establishes or knows the path followed by the sun.
Aruṇa serves as Sūrya’s charioteer and buffers the world from his heat.
Vāyu’s relation to Sūrya is mediated through his son Hanumān’s later education.

relations.myth: Sun and wind form cosmic counterparts
relations.note: Later Vedic systems correlate celestial Sūrya with atmospheric Vāyu and cosmic Prāṇa.
Viṣṇu and Indra jointly make or establish Sūrya.
Later theology worships the solar deity as Sūrya-Nārāyaṇa.
Viśvakarman reduces Sūrya’s unbearable brilliance after Saṃjñā flees.
Viśvakarman turns Sūrya on an apparatus and removes his unbearable brilliance.
Sūrya appears as a subordinate or neighboring image in the temple complex.
Vṛtra's defeat is associated with Indra's production or revelation of Sūrya.
Yama is named as Vivasvant’s son and later placed in the solar family.
Yamī, later identified with river-goddess Yamunā, is Sūrya’s daughter.
Yamuna or Kālindī is explicitly described as the Sun's daughter.
Some later traditions make Narakāsura the son of Varāha and Bhūdevī.

relations.myth: Viṣṇu joins the gods’ campaign against Tāraka
relations.note: Recension-dependent Purāṇic accounts have Tāraka withstand or counter Viṣṇu before Skanda attacks.
After her mortal marriage and transformation, Tulasi is divinely joined to Nārāyaṇa as a consort.
The plant is ceremonially married to Viṣṇu or his sacred stone representation.
Viṣṇu assumes or fabricates Jalandhara’s appearance so Vṛndā receives him as her husband.
Viṣṇu assumes Śaṅkhacūḍa’s form and enters Tulasi’s bed, breaking her protective fidelity.

relations.myth: Tulsi leaves and wreaths offered to Viṣṇu
relations.note: Viṣṇu wears tulsi wreaths and accepts the plant’s leaves as privileged offerings.
Vṛndā curses Viṣṇu after discovering his impersonation; consequences vary among recensions.
After exposing his impersonation, Tulasi curses Viṣṇu to assume a stone form.
The fragrance of tulsi from Viṣṇu’s feet spiritually transforms visiting sages.
Viṣṇu remains at Vṛndā’s pyre, grief-stricken or infatuated, and smears himself with her ashes.

relations.myth: Tulasi becomes river and sacred plant
relations.note: Viṣṇu declares that Tulasi’s body becomes the Gandakī and her hair becomes the sacred plant.
Viṣṇu prepares the womb while Tvaṣṭṛ fashions the embryo’s forms.
Viṣṇu becomes decisive in defeating or interpreting Vṛtra, Tvaṣṭṛ’s avenging creation.
One conflicting later genealogy treats Tvaṣṭṛ as a son of Viśvakarman.
Later Purāṇic and lexicographic traditions converge their identities and artisan functions.
Tvaṣṭṛ produces Vṛtra through sacrificial heat and formula to avenge Viśvarūpa.
Epic and Purāṇic retellings straightforwardly describe Vṛtra as Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
Later exegesis makes Yamī a child of Saraṇyū and thus Tvaṣṭṛ’s granddaughter.
Vāsuki serves as the churning rope during the horse’s emergence.
He initiates or enables the churning from which Uchchaihshravas emerges.

relations.myth: Kurma supports Mandara during the churning
relations.note: In tortoise form, Viṣṇu supports the mountain as Uchchaihshravas emerges.

relations.myth: Bali is bound with Varuṇa’s cords
relations.note: Varuṇa supplies the bonds or binding power used against Bali.
Vāmana is Viṣṇu’s dwarf incarnation and expands into his cosmic form.
Varuṇa refuses Hiraṇyākṣa’s challenge and directs him toward Viṣṇu, leading to Varāha’s battle.
Viṣṇu cooperates with Indra by bringing buffaloes, food, or spoils.

relations.myth: Vaiṣṇava assimilation of the cosmic boar
relations.note: Varāha becomes an avatāra or manifestation of Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa.
Vāyu and Varuṇa appear together as directional gods and members of divine assemblies.
Viśvakarman constructs Varuṇa's celestial assembly hall.
Yama and Varuṇa jointly appear as kings in Vedic funerary imagery.
Varuṇa joins Yama, Indra, and Agni as a divine suitor of Damayantī.
Yama invokes Varuṇa with Mitra concerning truth, ordinance, and divine observation.
Learned iconographic schemes place Yamuna and Ganga beside Varuṇa without a narrative encounter.

relations.myth: Vāyu and Vāsuki struggle around a mountain
relations.note: Vāyu’s wind tears away a mountain peak during a strength contest with Vāsuki.
Vāsuki serves as the churning rope while Vishnu stabilizes the operation.
One genealogy makes Viśvakarman the son of the Vasu Prabhāsa.
Viśvakarman is genealogically associated with the Vasus through Prabhāsa.

relations.myth: Vāyu serves as Viṣṇu’s chief mediator
relations.note: Madhva theology ranks Vāyu beneath Viṣṇu as his perfect servant and salvific mediator.
The Brahman-yaksha challenges Vāyu, who cannot move the offered straw.
Viśvakarman fashions Viṣṇu's discus from Sūrya's removed brilliance.
Sant poetry and Sanskrit māhātmyas identify Vithoba with supreme Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu stands beside Indra and enables his attack against Vṛtra.
Viṣṇu enters the sea foam Indra uses to kill Vṛtra.
Viṣṇu divides his power among Indra, the vajra, and earth for Vṛtra's destruction.
After Vṛtrāsura dies, his luminous essence reaches the supreme Lord.
Vṛtrāsura worships Nārāyaṇa and seeks only remembrance and divine service.
Yama acknowledges Viṣṇu’s supremacy and exempts devotees protected by his name.
Kālindī performs austerities seeking Viṣṇu, and Kṛṣṇa accepts her as his wife.
Kṛṣṇa crosses, plays beside, and sanctifies Yamunā throughout his childhood cycle.
Viśvakarman is Yamī-Yamunā’s maternal grandfather in Purāṇic solar genealogy.
After Yamī welcomes and feeds him, Yama grants a blessing for honored brothers.
Yamunā feeds Yama; he grants protections requested for those observing the sibling rite.
Yamī urges her twin to unite sexually, but Yama refuses.
Yamī proposes sexual union, but Yama rejects her on moral and kinship grounds.
Yamī cannot place Yama’s death in the past until night creates tomorrow.
Yamī is Yama’s twin sister.

Abhimānāsura.note: As Dhūmravarṇa, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying egoistic pride.

Abhramū.note: Directional-elephant lists pair Airāvata with the female elephant Abhramū.

Acala.note: Acala controls or converts Vināyaka in East Asian esoteric narratives.

Adharma.note: Some texts personify Adharma as an offspring or emanation of Brahmā.

Agastya.note: Later explanations link Urvaśī to Agastya’s birth from emitted seed deposited in a vessel.
Later accounts make Agastya a vessel-born offspring of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Later elaborations make Agastya arise with Vasiṣṭha from Mitra and Varuṇa’s contained seed.

Aghoreśvarī.note: Aghoreśvarī is the power and partner of Svacchandabhairava.

Aghāsura.note: Krishna expands inside the serpent-demon and kills him.

Agnihotra.note: Agnihotra is genealogized as Savitr and Pṛśni’s son.

Ahalyā.note: Indra approaches Ahalyā in Gautama’s form; her recognition and consent vary.
Lakshmana accompanies Rama when Ahalyā’s curse ends but does not liberate her.
Rāma releases Ahalyā from Gautama’s curse.

Ahi-ravana.note: Ahi-ravana abducts Lakshmana and Rama to sacrifice them in the underworld.

Aindrī.note: Aindrī joins the Mothers fighting Andhaka’s proliferating forms.
She struck him with a thunderbolt and mace, causing blood-born warriors to appear.
Aindrī kills the brothers’ troops with Indra’s thunderbolt.

Aiyaṉār.note: Cultic and learned systems treat Aiyaṉār and Ayyappa as cognate or identical.

Ajimā.note: At Asan Tol she converges with Newar grandmother and Jñāneśvarī traditions.

Akhilāṇḍeśvarī.note: The regional goddess is identified with Pārvatī as consort of a local Śiva.

Akṛtavraṇa.note: Akṛtavraṇa accompanies Paraśurāma and narrates his history in the Vana Parvan.

Akṣa.note: Akṣa is Ravana’s son, killed by Hanumān in Laṅkā.

Akṣobhya.note: Particular Tibetan lineages link black or other Jambhala forms with Akṣobhya.
The text assigns Akṣobhya as Tārā’s male partner.

Alakṣmī.note: Lakṣmī’s auspicious presence is opposed to Alakṣmī’s hunger and poverty.
Later mythology makes Alakṣmī Lakṣmī’s elder sister and fellow churning product.

All Gods.note: By awakening sacrifice, Uṣas renders service to the gods collectively.

Amba.note: Paraśurāma accepts Amba’s petition and champions her claim against Bhīṣma.

Ambarīṣa.note: Vishnu’s Sudarśana protects the devotee Ambarīṣa from Durvāsas.

Ambikā.note: A formerly distinct Rudra-associated goddess becomes a standard name for Śiva’s wife.
Ambikā appears with the Rudras and other divine hosts around Śiva.

Amitābha.note: Amitābha appears above or within iconographic lineages containing Hayagrīva.

Anaghā-Lakṣmī.note: Later vrata, mantra, and temple traditions jointly worship Anaghā-Lakṣmī beside Datta.

Anasūyā.note: Chandra is Anasūyā’s son in the three-brother birth tradition.
Anasūyā bears Dattātreya after Atri's austerities and the gods' response.
Anasūyā receives Sītā and instructs her about married conduct.
Anasūyā gives Sītā garments or ornaments.

Anavatapta.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Anavatapta.note: Anavatapta and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Aniruddha.note: Saṃkarṣaṇa and Aniruddha are fellow Vṛṣṇi heroes and Pāñcarātra emanations.
Balarama attends Aniruddha’s marriage connecting the Yādavas with Rukmin’s family.
Aniruddha is an important descendant, conventionally Krishna’s grandson through Pradyumna.
Aniruddha is indirectly styled Rati’s son through Pradyumna’s identity as Kāma.
Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa rescues his grandson Aniruddha during the conflict with Bāṇa.
Aniruddha is the fourth member of the Pāñcarātra emanational sequence.

Anuhlāda.note: Anuhlāda is listed among Hiranyakashipu’s sons.

Aparā.myth: Trika’s triadic manifestation of divine power
Aparā.note: Aparā expresses one aspect of Bhairava’s triadic power.

Apasmāra.note: Śiva dances upon the dwarf embodying forgetfulness or ignorance.

Apālā.note: Apālā offers Indra soma, and he heals her skin and fertilizes fields.

Aquatic female.note: An unnamed aquatic female is presented as the twins’ corresponding female ancestor.

Arajā.note: The later Uttarakāṇḍa names Arajā as Śukra’s daughter.

Arbuda.note: Indra defeats Arbuda among his named Rigvedic adversaries.

Ariṣṭa.note: Ariṣṭa belongs to Kamsa’s asura faction, though command sequences vary.
Late genealogical catalogues list Ariṣṭa among Mitra's children.

Ariṣṭanemi.note: Daksha gives daughters to Ariṣṭanemi in the sixty-daughter genealogy.

Ariṣṭā.note: The Bhāgavata derives Gandharvas from Kaśyapa and Ariṣṭā.

Ariṣṭāsura.myth: Radha challenges Krishna after Ariṣṭāsura’s death
Ariṣṭāsura.note: The demon’s death prompts Radha’s demand that Krishna purify himself.

Arjuna.note: Arjuna shields Agni from Indra’s rain and prevents inhabitants from escaping.
Urvaśī propositions Arjuna, who refuses her as an ancestress of his dynasty.
Urvaśī curses Arjuna to live without conventional manhood after he rejects her.
Balarama opposes or becomes angry at Arjuna’s taking of Subhadrā.
Arjuna defeats the Gandharva Aṅgāraparṇa with a fiery weapon.
After Arjuna spares him, the former opponent becomes an ally.
Aṅgāraparṇa instructs Arjuna and narrates genealogical traditions after their reconciliation.
Citrāsena teaches Arjuna song, dance, and instrumental performance in Indra’s heaven.
Arjuna confronts Citrāsena before their friendship permits the captives’ release.
Hanuman occupies Arjuna’s banner during the Kurukṣetra war.
Later tales pit Hanuman against Arjuna in a bridge-building contest.
Indra fathers Arjuna through Kuntī’s invocation.
Indra hosts Arjuna in heaven and supplies celestial weapons and martial instruction.
Krishna and Arjuna embody the divine pair Nārāyaṇa and Nara.
Krishna serves as Arjuna’s unarmed charioteer and secures Pāṇḍava victory.
Krishna teaches Arjuna action, knowledge, devotion, incarnation, and surrender.
Krishna and Arjuna jointly help Agni consume the Khāṇḍava forest.
Arjuna encounters Kubera and receives divine recognition or gifts in weapon-cycle traditions.
Ghaṭotkaca fights as Arjuna's rākṣasa nephew and Pāṇḍava ally.
Ghaṭotkaca's death expends Karṇa's divine missile and thereby saves Arjuna.

Arjuna.myth: Kirāta and Arjuna contest the boar
Arjuna.note: Disguised as a mountain hunter, Śiva fights and defeats Arjuna.
After revealing himself, Śiva grants Arjuna the catastrophic Pāśupata weapon.
Disguised as a Kirāta hunter, Śiva fights Arjuna over a slain boar.
Śiva reveals himself and awards Arjuna the Pāśupata weapon.
Varuṇa gives Arjuna Gāṇḍīva, inexhaustible quivers, and a divine chariot.
Varuṇa later grants Arjuna his divine weapon during Arjuna’s acquisition of celestial arms.
As Kṛṣṇa, Vishnu serves as Arjuna’s charioteer in the Kurukṣetra war.
Kṛṣṇa teaches Arjuna and reveals his cosmic form.
Arjuna ignores the yaksha’s warning, drinks from the lake, and falls apparently dead.
The yaksha restores Arjuna after Yudhiṣṭhira passes the test.
Arjuna meets Kālindī and conveys her wish to marry Kṛṣṇa.

Aryaka.note: Aryaka brings Bhīma before Vāsuki after recognizing his kinship.

Asiknī.note: Some later genealogies make Asiknī or Pañcajanī Aditi's mother.
Asiknī becomes the Prācetasa Daksha’s wife and bears sons and daughters.

Asiloman.note: A later Skandapurāṇa genealogy names Asiloman as Śumbha’s son.

Asuras, Daityas, and Dānavas.note: These anti-god collectives support Soma’s side under Śukra.

Atharvan.note: Atharvan is named as Brahmā's eldest son.
Brahmā teaches the knowledge of brahman to his eldest son Atharvan.

Atikāya.note: Atikāya is named among Ravana’s sons.

Atri.note: Atri is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Soma emerges from Atri’s eyes or tears after his austerities.
Variant accounts generate Soma from Atri’s concentrated ascetic radiance.
Dattātreya is born as the divine son of the sage Atri.
Indra and other gods help Atri escape affliction and restore the sun.
Atri is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.
Atri discovers or restores Sūrya after Svarbhānu conceals him.

Avalokiteśvara.note: Avalokiteśvara appears in conversion or emanation traditions involving Vināyaka.
Buddhist Hayagrīva is variously Avalokiteśvara’s attendant, wrathful emanation, or active power.

Aŋra Mainyu.myth: Vayu moves between the rival creations
Aŋra Mainyu.note: Iranian Vayu operates in the intermediate space between the good and evil creations.

Aśokasundarī.myth: Pārvatī produces Aśokasundarī from a wish-fulfilling tree
Aśokasundarī.note: A less widely attested tradition makes Aśokasundarī her created daughter.
Some later traditions name Aśokasundarī as a child of Śiva.
Particular later traditions name Aśokasundarī as Śiva’s child.

Aśvasena.note: Agni attempts to consume the nāga Aśvasena, who escapes the conflagration.

Aži Dahāka.note: Aži Dahāka petitions Vayu for victory, but Vayu refuses destructive claimants.

Aṃśa.note: Aṃśa is named within Aditi's Āditya collective.
Aṃśa is invoked with the collective as the divine portion.
Aṃśa and Bhaga are jointly enumerated among the Ādityas.
Aṃśa and Daksha are jointly invoked among the Ādityas.
Aṃśa and Mitra are jointly invoked as maintainers or distributors within divine order.

Aṅgada.note: Vāli’s son Aṅgada serves as Lakshmana’s ally during the Lanka campaign.
Aṅgada tells Sampāti about Jaṭāyu’s defense of Sītā and subsequent death.
Sampāti tells Aṅgada and his companions where Rāvaṇa holds Sītā.

Aṅgiras.note: Aṅgiras is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Aṅgiras is Bṛhaspati’s father in the established epic-Purāṇic genealogy.
Daksha gives daughters to Aṅgiras in the sixty-daughter genealogy.
Aṅgiras is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.

Aṅgirases.note: The groups compete for heaven through ritual preparation and reciprocal priestly service.
The Aṅgirases are called sons of Heaven in genealogical language.

Aṅgirases.myth: Release of cattle, dawn, and light
Aṅgirases.note: Their opening of the cattle-pen models the release of dawn and light.

Babhru.note: Purāṇic genealogies name Babhru as Sampāti’s son.

Bahāʾuʾllāh.note: Bahāʾī comparative theology presents Bahāʾuʾllāh as fulfilling the expectation of Viṣṇu’s tenth avatāra.

Baka Brahmā.note: As Buddha's opponent, Baka Brahmā has his limited knowledge and impermanent realm exposed.

Bakāsura.note: Krishna kills the crane-demon after it attempts to swallow him.

Bala.note: Bala joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Balvala.note: Balarama drags Balvala from the air and crushes him with his club.

Balāhaka.note: Balāhaka is named as a child of Kalki and Ramā.

Basava.note: Later Vīraśaiva hagiographies treat the historical teacher Basava as an incarnation of Nandi.

Batara Guru.note: Indonesian traditions identify Batara Guru with Śiva while reshaping him locally.

Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā.note: Pañcasikha sings of his love for the Gandhabba princess Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā.

Bhadrakālī.note: Bhadrakālī assists Śiva’s forces in destroying Daksha’s sacrifice.
Pāñcarātra theology identifies Bhadrakālī as a form of Mahālakṣmī.

Bhadrakālī.myth: Recurrent buffalo conflict in another cosmic cycle
Bhadrakālī.note: Bhadrakālī kills a form of Mahiṣa in one recurring cosmic cycle.

Bhadramadā.note: Bhadramadā is Airāvata’s maternal grandmother through Irāvatī.

Bhadrā.note: Bhadrā is commonly named as Kubera’s consort in later systematized traditions.

Bhagīratha.note: Śiva assists Bhagīratha by catching Gaṅgā’s destructive fall.

Bharadvāja.note: Some epic-Purāṇic variants make Bharadvāja the offspring of Bṛhaspati and Mamatā.

Bharata.note: Bharata is Rāma’s half-brother, born to Kaikeyī.
Bharata governs under Rāma’s sandals while awaiting his return.

Bhasmāsura.note: Śiva grants him a boon allowing destructive power by touch.

Bhasmāsura.myth: Bhasmāsura turns Śiva's boon against him
Bhasmāsura.note: The boon recipient threatens Śiva, requiring Viṣṇu or Mohinī's intervention.

Bhikṣāṭana.note: Medieval texts and images sometimes fuse Bhairava with Bhikṣāṭana features.

Bhāratī.note: Sarasvatī and Bhāratī appear together as distinguishable goddesses in early ritual.
Later exegesis and devotional practice often identify Bhāratī with Sarasvatī.

Bhīma.note: Balarama condemns Bhīma’s illegal thigh blow and raises his weapon against him.
Hanuman and Bhīma are half-brothers through their common father Vāyu.
Hanuman humbles Bhīma by making him unable to lift his tail.
Hanuman teaches Bhīma humility and reveals his immense expanded form.
Hanuman blesses Bhīma and promises to strengthen the Pāṇḍavas’ battle cries.
Krishna directs Bhīma’s strategy for killing Jarāsandha.
Bhīma fights Kubera’s yakṣas and kills Maṇimat in Kubera’s protected territory.
Kubera pardons Bhīma’s violence and welcomes him with the other Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīma kills the rākṣasas Hidimba, Baka, and Kirmīra.
The rākṣasī Hidimbā marries Bhīma under an agreed limitation.
Ghaṭotkaca, son of Hidimbā and Bhīma, belongs to the rākṣasa line.
Vāsuki welcomes Bhīma and permits him to drink a strength-giving elixir.

Bhīma.myth: Kuntī invokes Vāyu and conceives Bhīma
Bhīma.note: The epic presents Vāyu as Bhīma’s divine father and source of his strength.
Dvaita theology identifies Bhīma as Vāyu’s second incarnation serving Kṛṣṇa.
Bhīma ignores the yaksha’s warning, drinks from the lake, and falls apparently dead.
The yaksha restores Bhīma after Yudhiṣṭhira passes the test.
Bhīma fights yaksha guardians while intruding into Kubera’s Himalayan domain.

Bhīṣma.note: The cursed Vasu Dyu is born as Devavrata, later called Bhīṣma.
Ganga is the mother of Devavrata, later called Bhīṣma.
Ganga raises and educates Devavrata before returning him to Śāntanu.
Bhīṣma is portrayed as Paraśurāma’s pupil or acknowledged weapons disciple.
Paraśurāma fights Bhīṣma for weeks until divine and ancestral intervention ends the stalemate.
The surviving eighth child becomes Devavrata, later Bhīṣma, the human incarnation of Dyu.
Eight radiant Vasus communicate knowledge of the Prasvāpa weapon to Bhīṣma.
The Vasus prevent Bhīṣma from using Prasvāpa and help end his lethal duel.
After his mortal life, Bhīṣma is seen again among the Vasus.

Bhū.note: Hiraṇyākṣa claims Earth for the lower-world inhabitants while Varāha raises her.
Hiraṇyākṣa explicitly carries Earth away to Pātāla.

Bhūdevī.note: Brahmā hears Earth's complaint and convenes the gods to seek Viṣṇu's incarnation.
Bhūdevī and Śrīdevī appear as differentiated fellow consorts of Viṣṇu.
Bhūdevī flanks Matsya as Vedanārāyaṇa, representing Viṣṇu’s consort rather than Matsya’s independent wife.
Varāha finds Earth beneath the primeval waters and raises her.
Earth addresses Varāha as her lord and becomes his consort and interlocutor.
Earth takes sow form, unites with Varāha, and bears destructive offspring.
As Varāha, Vishnu raises Bhūdevī from the cosmic waters.
Earth appeals for Vishnu’s intervention against oppressive rulers burdening her.
Developed South Indian theology and iconography place Bhūdevī beside Vishnu as a consort.

Bhūmi.note: Earth’s appeal concerning oppressive rulers prompts Krishna’s divine descent.
Bhūmi praises Krishna and returns divine objects after Narakāsura is killed.

Bhūmi.myth: Earth nurses and raises the sweat-born child
Bhūmi.note: Earth mothers Mangala, who consequently becomes known as Bhauma, her son.
Later epic and devotional tradition treats Sītā as Earth’s daughter.

Bhūmi.myth: Final oath and return to Earth
Bhūmi.note: Bhūmi embraces Sītā upon a throne and takes her underground.
Earth gives Vāmana a black-deer skin.

Bhūta.note: Bhūta and Sarūpā are parents of a separately enumerated Rudra group.

Bhūtasantāpana.note: Some variable Purāṇic genealogical compilations list Bhūtasantāpana as his son.

Bhṛgu.note: Bhṛgu is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Bhṛgu accompanies Brahmā when Brahmā answers Hiranyakashipu’s austerity.
A Purāṇic genealogy names Lakṣmī as the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Bhṛgu retaliates by cursing Nandin and Śiva’s followers.
Paraśurāma belongs to Bhṛgu’s priestly lineage and is consequently called Bhārgava.
Bhṛgu is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.
Common epic and Purāṇic genealogy names Śukra as Bhṛgu’s son.
An alternative genealogy places Kavi between Bhṛgu and Śukra.
The Bhṛguvallī presents Bhṛgu as Varuṇa’s son.
Varuṇa guides Bhṛgu through contemplative inquiry into food, breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss.

Bhṛṅgi.note: She merges with Śiva, but Bhṛṅgi persists by becoming skeletal or three-legged.
Bhṛṅgi is a later attendant of Śiva.

Bhṛṅgiriṭi.note: Nandin and Bhṛṅgiriṭi appear as prominent gaṇas and fighting companions.

Bhṛṅgī.note: Śiva transforms the redeemed Andhaka into Bhṛṅgī, lord of the gaṇas.

Brahmahatyā.note: Personified Brahmanicide pursues Bhairava until his release at Kāśī.

Brahmā Sahampati.note: Brahmā and Śakra jointly honor the Buddha and become paired attendants in art.

Brahmāṇī.note: Brahmāṇī is Brahmā's female śakti and Mātrikā counterpart.
Kālī and Brahmāṇī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.
She struck him with Brahmā’s staff.
Brahmāṇī fights and destroys troops belonging to the brothers.

Brahmā’s gods and devas collectively.note: Vishnu answers the gods’ appeals by descending against Rāvaṇa, Kaṃsa, and other enemies.

Brāhmī.note: Brāhmī participates among the Mothers fighting Andhaka’s proliferating forms.

Buddhi.note: Gaṇeśa marries Buddhi after defeating Skanda in the race.

Buddhist Mātṛkās.note: Buddhist Mātṛkās share protective, child-seizing, ritual, and iconographic territory with Hindu Mothers.
Buddhist Mātṛkās.source: Northwestern Buddhist art and dhāraṇī literature

Bāṇa.note: Bāṇa is Bali’s eldest son in common genealogical traditions.
Bāṇa is a further descendant in many Purāṇic genealogies.
Later lists place Bāṇa among Kamsa’s associates without securely documenting personal meetings.
Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa defeats Bāṇa and cuts away most of his arms.
After defeating and mutilating Bāṇa, Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa permits him to live.

Bāṇāsura.note: Krishna defeats Bāṇa and his forces but spares him after Śiva intercedes.
Śiva protects his devotee Bāṇa against Kṛṣṇa and accepts the settlement.

Bāṣkala.note: Some Purāṇic genealogical lists add Bāṣkala as his son.

Bṛgu.note: Bṛgu curses Agni to become all-devouring after Agni truthfully identifies Pulomā.
Bṛgu kicks Vishnu’s chest while testing the gods; Vishnu’s forbearance proves his superiority.

Caitanya.note: Caitanya dances before Jagannath and experiences ecstatic divine identity and separation.
Gauḍīya theology identifies Caitanya as Krishna assuming Rādhā’s mood and complexion.

Caitanya.myth: Krishna assumes Radha’s emotion and complexion as Caitanya
Caitanya.note: Caitanya embodies Krishna experiencing Radha’s love and golden complexion.

Cakrasaṃvara.note: Newar Buddhists worship Cakrasaṃvara while participating in public Bhairava festivals.

Cakreśvarī.note: Garuḍa serves as the vehicle of the Jain yakṣī Cakreśvarī.

Camarendra.note: Śakra and Camara are distinguished as Indras governing different celestial classes.

Campakalatā.myth: Campakalatā coordinates Radha’s adornment and secret meetings
Campakalatā.note: She assists Radha with dress, messages, reconciliation, and rendezvous.

Candimā.note: Rāhu seizes the lunar deity but releases him upon the Buddha’s command.

Candrahantrī.note: Candrahantrī is listed among Siṃhikā’s children alongside Rāhu.

Candrapramardana.note: Candrapramardana is listed among Siṃhikā’s children alongside Rāhu.

Candravālī.myth: Krishna’s attention to Candravālī provokes Radha’s anger
Candravālī.note: Candravālī rivals Radha and embodies a contrasting mode of divine love.

Caṇḍa.note: Durgā’s wrath produces Kālī, who attacks and kills Caṇḍa.
Kālī battles Caṇḍa before decapitating him.
Kālī decapitates Caṇḍa and carries his head to Caṇḍikā.
This variant assigns the removal of Pūṣan’s teeth to Caṇḍa.

Caṇḍa.myth: Report and attempted capture of the Goddess
Caṇḍa.note: Caṇḍa reports the Goddess’s beauty, then is ordered by Śumbha to capture her.

Caṇḍikā.myth: Kālī emerges from Caṇḍikā’s angry brow
Caṇḍikā.note: Kālī erupts from the sovereign Goddess’s brow as embodied anger.
Caṇḍikā commands Kālī to consume Raktabīja’s blood and duplicates.
Caṇḍikā awards Kālī the name Cāmuṇḍā after receiving the demons’ heads.
The Mothers approach Caṇḍikā and fight the demon armies under her command.

Caṇḍikā.myth: Powers absorbed into the supreme Goddess
Caṇḍikā.note: The Mothers are comprehended within Caṇḍikā and withdraw into her before Śumbha’s duel.
Later Goddess theology links Caṇḍikā with Pārvatī while early narratives retain distinctions.
She devised the blood-catching strategy, resisted his mace, and wounded him.
She killed the blood-drained Raktabīja with her collected weapons.

Chenchata.note: Narasimha encounters the Chenchu huntress and seeks or contracts marriage with her.
The god-king Narasimha marries Vāsantikā with Lakṣmī’s acceptance.

Chinnamastā.note: Chinnamastā stands upon the copulating Rati and Kāma in Tantric iconography.

Chinnamuṇḍā.note: Chinnamastā and Buddhist Chinnamuṇḍā share self-decapitation, three blood streams, and two attendants.

Chāyā.note: Genealogies derive Sāvarṇi Manu from Chāyā or Savarṇā, the Sun’s substitute wife.
Chāyā bears Shani while serving as Saṃjñā’s shadow substitute.
Saṃjñā’s shadow-double becomes Sūrya’s substitute wife and bears his children.
Chāyā conceals the substitution until her unequal treatment exposes it.
Chāyā replaces or doubles Saṃjñā and becomes mother of Yama’s half-siblings.
Chāyā becomes Yamī’s surrogate mother or stepmother, without a substantial direct confrontation.
Chāyā is Yamuna's shadow-stepmother and cares for Saṃjñā's children after her departure.

Citragupta.note: The later divine accountant records deeds within Yama’s bureaucratic court.

Citraketu.note: Vṛtrāsura is revealed as the rebirth of the cursed king Citraketu.

Citrasena.note: Citrasena conveys to Urvaśī and Arjuna Indra’s arrangement for their encounter.

Citrā.myth: Citrā coordinates Radha’s adornment and secret meetings
Citrā.note: She assists Radha with dress, messages, reconciliation, and rendezvous.

Cloud deity.note: A banished yaksha commissions a personified monsoon cloud to carry a message to his wife.

Cosmic Person.myth: Moon arises from the cosmic Person’s mind
Cosmic Person.note: The moon is born from the cosmic Person’s mind.

Cumuri.note: Indra overcomes Cumuri in Rigvedic catalogues of martial victories.

Cyavana.note: Indra threatens Cyavana, who immobilizes or defeats him and secures soma for the Aśvins.

Cārvi.note: Cārvi occurs as Kubera’s consort in a variant later tradition.

Cāturmāsya.note: Cāturmāsya is genealogized as Savitr and Pṛśni’s son.

Cāṇūra.note: Kamsa’s supernaturalized champion fights Kṛṣṇa and is killed by him.

Dadhyañc.note: An obscure hymn associates Indra’s victory with Dadhyañc’s bones or horse-head.

Dadhīci.note: Dadhīci condemns Daksha’s exclusion of Śiva and abandons the rite.
Dadhīci relinquishes his body so the gods can forge Indra’s vajra.
Later narratives join Dadhīci’s donated bones with Tvaṣṭṛ’s weapon-making domain.

Daityas and Dānavas.note: The Ādityas fight these rival divine populations for sovereignty and immortality.

Daivajña.note: Community genealogies name Daivajña among Viśvakarman's five artisan sons.

Dakṣiṇāmūrti.note: The text assigns five-faced Dakṣiṇāmūrti as Bhairavī’s partner.

Dantavakra.note: Dantavakra is Vijaya’s birth paired with Jaya’s birth as Śiśupāla.

Dawn.note: The creator sexually desires or unites with his daughter, identified as Dawn or Sky.

Day.note: Personified Day returns the protected worshippers to shining Night.

Daśaratha.note: Rāma is the eldest son of King Daśaratha of Kosala.

Devahūti.note: Devahūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.

Devakī.note: Balarama begins as Devakī’s seventh embryo before transfer to Rohiṇī.
As Kṛṣṇa, Jagannath is the son of Devakī.
Krishna is Devakī’s eighth child in the developed birth cycle.

Devakī.myth: Śeṣa embryo first resides in Devakī
Devakī.note: In his Balarāma incarnation, Śeṣa initially gestates within Devakī.
Vithoba inherits Kṛṣṇa’s mother through identification with Kṛṣṇa.

Devas.note: Apsarases emerge as devas and asuras churn the ocean; devas do not marry them.
The Devas support Bṛhaspati and oppose Soma’s coalition.
Vāsuki serves as the churning rope used by the gods and Asuras.
Brāhmaṇa and Upaniṣadic accounts describe the gods collectively as Prajāpati's children.
Prajāpati's syllable da teaches the gods self-restraint.
The gods condemn Prajāpati's union with his daughter and commission his punishment.
The devas enlist Vāsuki as their churning rope and pull his tail.
The gods support Vāsuki’s plea to Brahmā concerning the threatened nāgas.

Devasenā.note: One epic account has Skanda rescue or receive Devasenā.
Skanda marries Devasenā, daughter or ward of Indra.

Devayānī.note: Devayānī is Śukra’s daughter and central to his epic biography.

Devāntaka.note: Devāntaka is named among Ravana’s sons.

Devāpi.note: The immortal Devāpi resumes Lunar dynastic authority under Kalki’s restored order.

Devī.note: Apsarases join the celestial celebration following Devī’s victories.
Śākta cosmologies subordinate Prajāpati's creator function, through Brahmā, to the supreme Goddess.
Śākta theology subsumes Earth as a manifestation or material power of supreme Devī.

Dhanuka.note: A later Skandapurāṇa genealogy names Dhanuka as Śumbha’s son.

Dharaṇendra.note: Dharaṇendra occupies the nadir below the eight in some Jain directional systems.

Dharma.note: Some texts personify Dharma as an offspring or emanation of Brahmā.
Daksha gives Dharma ten or thirteen daughters, depending on the genealogy.
Personified Dharma joins Kalki’s side and is restored through his victory.
An epic genealogical variant names Kāma as Dharma’s son.
Purāṇic genealogies make Dharma father of all eight Vasus.
The lake yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira’s divine father.
Later traditions increasingly equate Yama with Dharma through judgment and Yudhiṣṭhira’s paternity.

Dhatarattha.note: Vessavaṇa acts jointly with Dhatarattha as one of the Four Great Kings.

Dhenuka.note: Balarama whirls the donkey demon by his hind legs into a tree.
Dhenuka is named among Kamsa-aligned asuras and killed by Balarāma.
Krishna participates while Balarāma principally kills the donkey-demon.

Dhruva.note: The celestial stream contacts Dhruva’s station during its cosmic descent.
Nārada tests Dhruva, then teaches him a mantra and worship of Vāsudeva.
Nārada initiates the resolute child into disciplined devotion to Vāsudeva.
The sages occupy a celestial circuit below or around Dhruva’s polar station.
Some late texts make the Seven Sages teachers of Dhruva.
Vishnu appears to the child ascetic and grants him an imperishable celestial station.
A yaksha kills Dhruva’s brother Uttama, provoking Dhruva’s attack upon Alakā.
Dhruva wages indiscriminate war against Alakā’s yakshas, who counterattack with magical illusions and storms.

Dhuni.note: Indra overcomes Dhuni in Rigvedic catalogues of martial victories.

Dhāminī.note: Modern harmonizations name Dhāminī as the wife whose curse makes Shani’s gaze destructive.

Dhātṛ.note: Dhātṛ places the embryo while Tvaṣṭṛ fashions its differentiated forms.

Dhūmorṇā.note: Iconographic traditions occasionally identify Dhūmorṇā as Yama’s consort.

Dhūmralocana.note: Durgā reduces Dhūmralocana to ash with her utterance.
Śumbha orders Dhūmralocana to seize the Goddess and kill her protectors.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra.note: Buddhist Gandharvas form the eastern retinue of the guardian king Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra Nāga.note: Airāvata is Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s Vedic patronymic; identity with the elephant remains unproved.

Dhṛṣṭa.note: Dhṛṣṭa appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Dievo sūneliai.note: Comparative scholarship links these Baltic divine sons with the Indo-European horse-twin complex.

Dioskouroi.note: Comparativists equate the pairs through horses, sea rescue, twinhood, and solar-maiden associations.

Diti.note: Later genealogies make Diti Aditi's sister and fellow wife of Kaśyapa.

Diti.myth: Aditi and Diti divide divine lineages
Diti.note: Diti, Aditi’s sister and co-wife, bears the rival Daityas.
Bali is a Daitya because he descends from Diti.
Diti is named among Daksha’s daughters and mothers the Daityas.
The slain Veda-thief is called ditija, implying descent from Diti.
Diti is Hiranyakashipu’s mother, making him a Daitya.
Diti bears Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu after conceiving with Kaśyapa.
Indra serves Diti while awaiting a lapse in her ritual purity.
Indra enters Diti’s womb and divides the fetus intended to kill him.
Diti conceives the embryo that becomes seven Marut groups after Indra divides it.
Diti’s divided embryo becomes forty-nine Maruts in the elaborated Purāṇic genealogy.
Later summaries loosely place Tāraka among Diti’s descendants.

Divodāsa.note: The received medical recension identifies King Divodāsa, Suśruta’s teacher, as Dhanvantari incarnate.

Droṇa.note: Paraśurāma gives Droṇa his complete weapons knowledge, including deployment and withdrawal.

Durgama.note: The Goddess fights Durgama after his seizure of Vedic power causes drought.
She kills Durgama and recovers the Vedas.
The emitted Mahāvidyās join Śākambharī’s forces against Durgama.

Durvāsas.note: Airāvata discards Durvāsas’s garland, provoking a curse upon Indra or the gods.
Durvāsas is Chandra’s brother in the Atri–Anasūyā birth cycle.
Durvāsas and Dattātreya are co-born sons of Atri and Anasūyā.

Durvāsas.myth: Durvāsas’s curse precipitates the churning crisis
Durvāsas.note: His curse on Indra indirectly causes the crisis requiring Kūrma’s manifestation.
Lakshmana admits the threatening sage, sacrificing himself to prevent a kingdom-wide curse.
His curse after Indra mistreats the garland precipitates Lakṣmī’s withdrawal.
Vishnu’s discus pursues Durvāsas after the sage threatens Ambarīṣa.

Duryodhana.note: Some traditions make Balarama Duryodhana’s mace-fighting teacher or special authority.

Dyu.note: Tradition associates Dyaus with the Vasu Dyu, though strict identity is unproved.

Dyu.myth: Dyu steals Nandinī for her miraculous milk
Dyu.note: Dyu steals Nandinī at his wife’s request, prompting Vasiṣṭha’s curse.

Dyāvā-Pṛthivī.note: Heaven and Earth are asked to grant freedom or security; Aditi's personification is disputed.

Dīrghatamas.note: Bṛhaspati curses the unborn Dīrghatamas with blindness after he protests the intercourse.

Dūṣaṇa.note: Lakshmana participates in the conflict, while Rama performs the chief slaughter.

Dṛḍhā.note: Sarasvatī and the earth goddess cooperate in protecting the Buddhist scripture.

Earth.note: Earth cannot withstand Ganga’s unrestrained fall from heaven.

Earth.myth: Earth appeals for relief from adharma
Earth.note: Earth complains of adharma’s burden, helping prompt Kalki’s divine descent.
After conquering Earth, Paraśurāma gives her as a sacrificial donation to Kaśyapa.
Earth occurs among Prajāpati's alternative feminine creative partners.

Earth goddess.note: Earth receives Sītā; grieving Rāma protests and threatens the goddess.

Ekanāṃśā.note: Some traditions identify Kṛṣṇa’s escaped substitute sister with Ekanāṃśā.

Elāpatra.note: Elāpatra tells Vāsuki that Jaratkāru’s future son will save the serpents.

Emūṣa.note: The ritual boar Emūṣa lifts Earth from the primordial waters.

Erāvana Nāga.note: A homonymous nāga appears independently; identification with Sakka’s elephant remains optional and fluid.

Four Heavenly Kings.note: Sarasvatī and the Four Heavenly Kings serve as co-protectors of scripture and polity.

Four Kumāras.note: Their curse remotely causes the gatekeepers’ births as Ravana and Kumbhakarṇa.
Their curse on Jaya and Vijaya indirectly prepares Varāha’s confrontation with Hiraṇyākṣa.

Fūten.note: Indian Vāyu entered East Asian Buddhism as the directional or elemental deity Fūten.

Gajanan Maharaj.note: Some modern Datta organizations incorporate Gajanan Maharaj into Dattātreya incarnation lists.

Gajendra.note: Garuḍa transports Viṣṇu to Gajendra but does not himself grant liberation.
Vishnu frees the surrendered elephant devotee from a crocodile.

Gajāsura.note: Kapālin-led Rudras participate in killing the elephant demon Gajāsura.

Gandabheruṇḍa.note: Narasimha transforms into the two-headed bird Gandabheruṇḍa to overcome Śarabha.
Vaiṣṇava counternarratives make Gandabheruṇḍa a further Vishnu form opposing Śarabha.

Gandharva Viśvāvasu.note: Viśvāvasu leaves the married woman while Aryaman helps establish her new union.

Garuḍī.note: Some later or regional traditions name Garuḍī as Garuḍa's wife.

Gaurī.note: Distinct fair, agricultural and regional goddess traditions become identified with Pārvatī.

Gautama.note: Indra assumes Gautama’s appearance to gain access to Ahalyā.
Gautama catches and curses Indra, causing him to lose his testicles.

Gaveṣṭhin.note: A conflicting later genealogy makes Śumbha and Niśumbha sons of Gaveṣṭhin.

Ghora Āṅgirasa.note: Ghora Āṅgirasa gives esoteric instruction to Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra, whose identification remains uncertain.

Gomedha.note: Some Jain image labels identify Gomedha with Kuvera, but the equation remains contested.

Gulika.note: South Indian astrological practice sometimes calls the upagraha Gulika Shani’s son.

Gāndharvī.note: A Purāṇic taxonomic genealogy places Uchchaihshravas among horses descended from Gāndharvī.

Gāndhārī.note: Gāndhārī curses Krishna after the Kurukṣetra war, foreshadowing Yādava destruction.

Gāyatrī.note: Brahmā marries or installs Gāyatrī as ritual wife so the sacrifice can proceed.

Hariṇaigameṣin.note: Śakra commands Hariṇaigameṣin to transfer Mahāvīra’s embryo between mothers.

Haryaśvas.note: Daksha fathers five thousand Haryaśvas to populate the cosmos.

Harṣa.note: Rati or her genealogical form Nandī is Harṣa’s mother.
Harṣa is named as a son of Kāma and Rati.

Hayagrīva.note: Hayagrīva’s head is fused into the five-faced form of Hanuman.
Lakṣmī is joined with Viṣṇu’s horse-headed form in learning traditions.
In some versions Vishnu confronts the demon Hayagrīva who stole the Vedas.
Other versions identify Hayagrīva as Vishnu’s horse-headed form recovering the Vedas.

Heaven.note: Heaven gives Vāmana the umbrella carried to Bali’s sacrifice.

Heaven and Earth.note: Ṛgvedic poetry describes Agni as born from Heaven and Earth.

Heruka.note: Newar Buddhists worship Heruka while participating in public Bhairava festivals.

Himavat.note: As Pārvatī, Annapūrṇā inherits Himavat as her father.
As Pārvatī, Durgā is treated as the daughter of Himavat.
Himavat supplies the Goddess with a lion and jewels.
Ganga is named Himavat’s elder daughter.

Himavat.myth: Gods equip the Goddess for war
Himavat.note: Himavat gives the Goddess her lion and jewels for the war against Mahiṣa.
Epic and Purāṇic traditions make her the mountain-god’s daughter.
Śākta theology presents the Goddess teaching her nominal mountain father.
After abandoning Satī’s body, the Goddess is born as Himavat’s daughter.

Himālaya.note: The sages visit Himālaya and negotiate his daughter Pārvatī’s marriage to Śiva.

Hiraṇyagarbha.note: Later tradition identifies the primordial Hiraṇyagarbha with Prajāpati and Brahmā.
Later exegesis identifies the primordial Hiraṇyagarbha with Prajāpati.

Hlāda.note: Hlāda is listed among Hiranyakashipu’s sons.

Holikā.note: Later festival folklore makes the demoness Holikā his sister.
Holikā collaborates in his attempt to burn Prahlāda but dies in the pyre.

Hārītī.note: Early Buddhist contexts depict Kubera-like abundance figures with Hārītī.
Hārītī functionally converges with the Mothers as both child-seizing and child-protecting goddess.
The yaksha general Pañcika is paired with Hārītī in Buddhist cult and Gandharan art.

Idumban.myth: Idumban challenges the child ascetic at Palani
Idumban.note: Murukaṉ fights Idumban when the latter attempts to move the two hills.
Murukaṉ kills Idumban during their struggle at Palani.
After killing Idumban, Murukaṉ restores him at divine request.
The restored Idumban serves as guardian and patron of burden-bearing devotees.

Idā.myth: Idā arises from Manu’s post-flood offering
Idā.note: Manu’s water-offering generates Idā, who becomes the blessing of his regenerative sacrifice.

Idā.myth: Idā identifies herself as Manu’s daughter
Idā.note: The woman generated from Manu’s offering explicitly identifies herself as his daughter.

Ikṣvāku.note: Vaivasvata Manu fathers Ikṣvāku, founder of the Solar Dynasty’s principal royal line.

Ilavilā.note: The dominant genealogy names Ilavilā, under variant names, as Kubera’s mother.

Ilā.note: Budha encounters Ilā in female form, and they conceive Purūravas.
Later genealogies make Ilā or Sudyumna Manu’s child, with sex and birth varying by account.

Indrajit.note: Garuḍa nullifies the serpent weapon with which Indrajit bound the two heroes.
Indrajit captures Hanuman with the Brahmāstra after Hanuman devastates the grove.
Indrajit wounds and magically binds Lakshmana before their decisive duel.
Lakshmana invokes Rama’s righteousness and beheads Indrajit with a divine missile.

Indrāṇī.note: Bṛhaspati shelters and counsels Indrāṇī when Nahusha attempts to obtain her.
Indrāṇī is Indra’s principal consort in later Vedic, epic, and Purāṇic literature.
Kālī and Indrāṇī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.

Indulekhā.myth: Indulekhā coordinates Radha’s messages and secret meetings
Indulekhā.note: She assists Radha with dress, messages, reconciliation, and rendezvous.

Irāvatī.note: Irāvatī bears the great elephant Airāvata.

Ištar.note: Both are attached to Venus in distinct astral systems, not narrative mythology.

Iḷā.note: Sarasvatī and Iḷā are jointly invited with Bhāratī in sacrificial hymns.

Jain Ambikā.note: Gaṇeśa appears as a subordinate attendant in some Jain Ambikā ensembles.

Jalandhara.note: Śiva battles and kills Jalandhara after Viṣṇu's deception weakens the demon.
Jalandhara.source: Padma, Skanda, and Śiva Purāṇa variants

Jalandhara.note: Vṛndā is Jalandhara’s wife, and her fidelity sustains or reinforces his invulnerability.

Jamadagni.note: Later Purāṇic accounts make Kamadhenu or Homadhenu the cow sustaining Jamadagni’s hermitage.
Paraśurāma is the son of the Bhṛgu sage Jamadagni.
He obeys Jamadagni’s command to behead Reṇukā after his brothers refuse.

Jambha.note: Jambha is commonly named as the father of Hiranyakashipu’s wife Kayādhu.

Jaratkāru.note: The nāga woman Jaratkāru is Vāsuki’s sister.

Jaratkāru.myth: Marriage arranged to save the nāgas
Jaratkāru.note: Vāsuki raises his sister and gives her in marriage to fulfill prophecy.

Jarā.note: The hunter Jarā mistakes Krishna’s foot for a deer and fatally shoots him.

Jarāsandha.note: Balarama and Kṛṣṇa repeatedly defeat Jarāsandha’s armies without killing him.
Krishna opposes Jarāsandha and devises the strategy by which Bhīma kills him.
In Jain universal history Krishna personally kills the Prativāsudeva Jarāsandha.
Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa participates in repeated conflicts with Jarāsandha.

Jaya.note: Jaya joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.
Hiranyakashipu is identified as Jaya’s first hostile birth away from Viṣṇu.
Jaya is named as a son of Kalki and Padmāvatī.
Killing Jaya’s enemy-incarnation Hiraṇyakaśipu advances the gatekeeper’s return to Viṣṇu.
Jaya fights or restrains Bali’s Asura forces as Vāmana’s attendant.
Jaya serves as one of Vishnu’s gatekeepers.
Vishnu repeatedly kills Jaya during the gatekeeper’s cursed births as divine enemies.

Jaya and Vijaya.note: Hiraṇyākṣa is one of the pair’s first births, without secure individual mapping.

Jaya and Vijaya.myth: Second birth of the cursed gatekeepers
Jaya and Vijaya.note: Ravana and Kumbhakarṇa are identified as the gatekeepers’ second demonic births.
Their cursed births cause Varāha’s confrontation with Hiraṇyākṣa, though Varāha does not meet their gatekeeper forms.

Jayanta.note: Jayanta is recurrently named as a child of Indra, though traditions vary.

Jayanti.note: Jayanti is recurrently named as Indra’s daughter, with varying narrative functions.

Jayantī.note: Indra’s daughter lives invisibly with Śukra for ten years.

Jayantī.myth: Jayantī attends Śukra during his austerity
Jayantī.note: Indra sends Jayantī to serve or distract Śukra during his penance.

Jhūlelāl.note: Sindhi Hindu tradition identifies the Indus-associated patron Jhūlelāl with Varuṇa.

Jālandhara.note: Nandin leads troops and fights commanders in Jālandhara’s army.

Jāmbavatī.note: Krishna marries Jāmbavatī after fighting her father Jāmbavān.

Jāmbavān.note: Jāmbavān reminds Hanuman of his forgotten strength and prompts his leap.
Krishna fights Jāmbavān over the Syamantaka jewel until Jāmbavān recognizes him.
After recognizing Krishna, Jāmbavān gives him Jāmbavatī in marriage.
Jāmbavān serves as an allied elder in Lakshmana’s joint martial campaign.
The ancient bear-chief counsels Rāma’s allied forces.
Sampāti answers Jāmbavān’s questions about Sītā’s location and her abductor.
Jāmbavān proclaims or sounds a trumpet celebrating Vāmana’s cosmic victory.

Ka.note: Ritual exegesis reified the hymn's interrogative Ka as Prajāpati.

Kabandha.note: Lakshmana and Rama sever Kabandha’s arms and release his celestial form.
Released Kabandha directs Lakshmana and Rama toward Sugriva.

Kabandha Śiva.myth: Headless Kabandha Śiva worshipped beside Chinnamastā
Kabandha Śiva.note: The text prescribes worship of headless Kabandha Śiva beside Chinnamastā.

Kaca.note: Kaca is Bṛhaspati’s eldest son and an agent of the devas.
Kaca advances his father’s divine priesthood by infiltrating Śukra’s school.
Śukra accepts Kaca as a pupil and teaches him mṛta-sañjīvanī.
Śukra repeatedly restores Kaca after the Asuras kill him.
Kaca tears out through Śukra’s body, necessarily killing his teacher.
Kaca uses the resurrection formula to restore Śukra after emerging.

Kadru.note: Kadru is the principal mother of the Nāga race.
Kadru curses disobedient Nāga sons to perish in Janamejaya's sacrifice.
Kadru fraudulently makes his white tail appear black to win her wager.

Kadrū.note: Variable later genealogies list Kadrū as Aditi's sister and co-wife.
Kadrū is named among Daksha’s daughters and becomes mother of nāgas.
Garuḍa carries Kadrū under the conditions of his mother's servitude.
Kadrū's sons demand amṛta from Garuḍa as Vinatā's ransom.
Śeṣa is born among Kadrū’s immense brood of serpent sons.

Kadrū.myth: Śeṣa repudiates his serpent family’s malice
Kadrū.note: Śeṣa abandons his mother’s malicious serpent offspring and undertakes austerities.
Kadrū is Vāsuki’s mother in the epic nāga genealogy.
Kadrū curses her resistant serpent sons; Vāsuki seeks to avert their destruction.

Kadutha.note: Kadutha is named among the guardian attendants associated with Ayyappa.

Kaikasī.note: Kaikasī is Ravana’s mother in the later epic genealogy.

Kaiṭabha.note: Threatened by Kaiṭabha, Brahmā invokes Mahāmāyā so Viṣṇu awakens and kills him.
She awakens Viṣṇu, enabling him to fight and kill Kaiṭabha.
Horse-headed Nārāyaṇa kills Kaiṭabha after recovering the Vedas.
Her withdrawal awakens Viṣṇu, indirectly enabling Kaiṭabha’s defeat and death.

Kaiṭabha.myth: Kaiṭabha threatens the Anantaśayana creation scene
Kaiṭabha.note: Kaiṭabha threatens Brahmā or confronts divine weapons beneath Viṣṇu and Śeṣa.
Vishnu kills the primordial-water demon Kaiṭabha alongside Madhu.

Kaliya.note: The nāga occupies Yamuna's pool and poisons her water, banks, animals, and vegetation.

Kamalākṣa.note: Kamalākṣa is one of Tāraka’s three sons and Tripura rulers.

Kanakhalā.note: Buddhist traditions associate Chinnamuṇḍā’s self-decapitation imagery with the adept Kanakhalā.

Kankālamūrti.note: The Viśvaksena cycle and later iconography sometimes fuse Bhairava with Kankālamūrti.

Karambha.note: Karambha is Rambha's brother and thus Mahiṣa's paternal uncle.

Karkoṭaka.note: Karkoṭaka is one of Śeṣa’s named nāga brothers.

Karkoṭaka.myth: Nāgas receive Balarāma’s returning serpent essence
Karkoṭaka.note: Karkoṭaka receives the thousand-headed serpent emerging from Balarāma at death.
Karkoṭaka is listed among Vāsuki’s brothers or close serpent kin.

Karūṣa.note: Karūṣa appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Karṇa.note: Disguised as a Brahmin, Indra obtains Karṇa’s congenital armor and earrings.
Indra compensates Karṇa with a one-use Śakti weapon for his armor.
Paraśurāma teaches Karṇa advanced weapons after Karṇa presents himself as a Brahmin.
Karṇa conceals his status until extraordinary endurance reveals the deception to Paraśurāma.
Paraśurāma curses Karṇa’s weapon knowledge to fail when most needed at death.
Karṇa kills Ghaṭotkaca with Indra's one-use Śakti weapon.
Sūrya fathers Karṇa, who is born with divine armor and earrings.
Sūrya grants his son natural divine armor and earrings at birth.
Sūrya warns Karṇa that disguised Indra will request his protective armor.

Karṇikāra.note: The Padma Purāṇa names Karṇikāra as a son of Jatāyu.

Kasubarasa.note: A Malay version makes Jentayu Kasubarasa the sage Kasubarasa’s son.

Kauberī.note: Kauberī occurs as Kubera’s consort in a variant later tradition.

Kaumārī.note: Kaumārī participates among the Mothers fighting Andhaka’s proliferating forms.
Kālī and Kaumārī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.

Kaumārī.myth: Kaumārī fights among the goddess’s Mātṛkās
Kaumārī.note: Kaumārī is the female power or śakti corresponding to Kumāra.
She wounded him with her spear or śakti.
Kaumārī, Skanda’s feminine power, fights the brothers’ army.

Kausalyā.note: Kausalyā bears Rāma after receiving part of the consecrated food.

Kauśikī.myth: Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī’s bodily sheath
Kauśikī.note: A radiant warrior goddess issues from Pārvatī while retaining a distinct identity.

Kavi.note: Kavi is named as one of Kalki’s brothers.
Some genealogies make Śukra the son or descendant of Kavi.

Kavyamātā.note: Later Purāṇic organization identifies Kavyamātā or Divyā as Śukra’s mother.

Kayādhu.note: Kayādhu is his wife; some dramatic and vernacular traditions call her Līlāvatī.
Nārada intervenes when Indra abducts Kayādhu and shelters her during pregnancy.

Kaśyapa.note: Epic and Purāṇic genealogies make Aditi a wife of Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa hears Aditi's grief and teaches her the milk-centered vow.
Aditi and Kaśyapa jointly enable Viṣṇu's incarnation as their son.
Epic and Purāṇic genealogies make Kaśyapa father of the Ādityas.
Extended epic-Purāṇic genealogies make Kaśyapa a remote ancestor; recensions differ.
An epic genealogy makes apsarases daughters of Kaśyapa and Pradhā.
Epic and Purāṇic genealogies make Aryaman a son of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Bali belongs to Kaśyapa’s Daitya lineage through Diti.
Kaśyapa joins Aditi in requesting Viṣṇu’s incarnation to end Bali’s rule.
Daksha gives Kaśyapa thirteen or more daughters who mother many species.
Several epic and Purāṇic genealogies make Gandharvas children or descendants of Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa fathers Garuḍa and Aruṇa by Vinatā.
Aśvagrīva appears among the Dānavas descended through Kaśyapa and Danu.
Hayagrīva is explicitly listed among the sons of Kaśyapa and Danu.
Kaśyapa is Hiranyakashipu’s father in the dominant Purāṇic genealogy.
Purāṇic genealogies identify Kaśyapa as Hiraṇyākṣa’s father.
Surabhi bears Nandinī through union with Kaśyapa.
An alternate transferred genealogy makes Ketu the son of Siṃhikā and Kaśyapa.
The Brāhmaṇa declares Kūrma equivalent to Kaśyapa through ritual etymology.
Kaśyapa fathers Diti’s pregnancy, from which the seven Marut groups arise.
Kaśyapa fathers Diti’s pregnancy and prescribes the vow preceding the Maruts’ birth.
Purāṇic genealogies make Kaśyapa Mitra's father through his marriage to Aditi.
The Nāgas are principally descended from Kaśyapa through Kadru.
Some bovinizing genealogies supply Kaśyapa as Nandin’s father.
Paraśurāma gives the conquered earth to Kaśyapa after completing his campaigns.
Kaśyapa orders Paraśurāma to leave the territory he has already donated.
Kaśyapa functions as a Prajāpati and fathers many divine and nonhuman lineages.
Later standard genealogies name Kaśyapa as Pūṣan’s father.
One Purāṇic genealogy makes Kaśyapa father of rākṣasas through Khasā.
Some epic-Purāṇic systems make the eleven Rudras offspring of Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa fathers the Rudras with Surabhi in several epic-Purāṇic genealogies.
Kaśyapa fathers the Rudras with Aditi in another genealogical tradition.
The standard genealogy makes Sampāti a descendant of Kaśyapa through Vinatā and Aruṇa.
Purāṇic genealogy names Kaśyapa as Savitr’s father.
Kaśyapa fathers Śeṣa and the other nāgas through Kadrū.
Epic-Purāṇic genealogy makes Sūrya the son of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Vāmana is born as the son of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Kaśyapa participates in Vāmana’s initiation and gives him the ritual girdle.
Purāṇic genealogies conventionally name Kaśyapa as Varuṇa’s father.
Kaśyapa is Vāsuki’s father in the nāga genealogy.
Alternative creation catalogues connect the Vasus with Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Kaśyapa fathers Vishnu’s Vāmana manifestation in the developed narrative.
Some Purāṇic genealogical variants derive the yakshas through Kaśyapa.

Kaṇḍu.note: Pramlocā unites with the sage Kaṇḍu in a Purāṇic ascetic-disruption narrative.

Kesarī.note: Kesarī is Añjanā’s husband and Hanuman’s social father.

Keśin.note: Kamsa sends Keśin to attack Kṛṣṇa after learning his identity.

Khara.note: Lakshmana participates in the crisis, though Rama performs the chief slaughter.

Khasā.note: One Purāṇic genealogy makes Khasā mother of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Some Purāṇic genealogical variants derive the yakshas through Khasā.

Khyāti.note: A Purāṇic genealogy names Khyāti as Lakṣmī’s mother.

Kichijōten.note: Buddhist transmission adapted Śrī-Lakṣmī as an East Asian fortune goddess.

Kisshōten.note: Their state-protection and fortune roles overlap, compete, or converge without a fixed personal narrative.

Koka.note: Kalki kills Koka simultaneously with Vikoka because each revives while the other lives.

Korravai.note: Early Tamil tradition describes the victory goddess Korravai as Murukaṉ’s mother.
Murukaṉ’s early Tamil mother Korravai was later equated with Durgā or Pārvatī.

Koṟṟavai.myth: Competing traditions name each goddess Murukaṉ’s mother
Koṟṟavai.note: Tamil tradition gives Koṟṟavai an alternative maternity later assimilated to Pārvatī’s family.

Kratu.note: Kratu is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Kratu is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.

Krauñca.myth: Skanda pierces Krauñca with his spear
Krauñca.note: Skanda pierces Krauñca, variously understood as mountain, demon, or both.

Krodhavaśā.note: Variable later genealogies list Krodhavaśā as Aditi's sister and co-wife.
Extended genealogies make Krodhavaśā a remote ancestor through varying intervening daughters.

Krodhāsura.note: As Lambodara, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying anger.

Kronos.note: Greek astral science equated Kronos and Shani by their shared planetary slot, not mythology.

Kumbhakarṇa.note: Brahmā grants or modifies Kumbhakarṇa's boon, resulting in prolonged sleep.
Kumbhakarṇa is Vijaya’s birth paired with Jaya’s birth as Rāvaṇa.
Kumbhakarṇa is Kubera’s paternal half-brother in the dominant genealogy.
Kumbhakarṇa is Ravana’s brother and fellow boon-seeking ascetic.

Kumbhīnasī.note: Kumbhīnasī is the wife who begs Arjuna to spare Citraratha.

Kumuda.note: Kumuda joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Kumudākṣa.note: Kumudākṣa joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Kumārī.note: Bhairava displays, dances, and sacrifices accompany the Kumārī procession.

Kuntī.note: Kuntī invokes Indra through her boon and conceives Arjuna by him.

Kuvalayāpīḍa.myth: Elephant ambush at the arena gate
Kuvalayāpīḍa.note: Kamsa stations the elephant to crush Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma before the contest.

Kuyava.note: Indra defeats Kuyava among his named Rigvedic adversaries.

Kuśa.note: Kuśa is a son of Rāma and Sītā.
Sītā gives birth to Kuśa during exile at Vālmīki’s hermitage.

Kāl nemi.note: Nandin engages Kāl nemi among Jālandhara’s demon commanders.

Kāla.note: Lakshmana guards the door under Kāla’s lethal non-interruption condition.
The hymn presents Āditya as encompassing divine Time.
Kāla may be Yama’s synonym, a superior cosmic force, or a separate death power.

Kālabhairava.note: Kālabhairava appears as a subordinate or neighboring image in the temple complex.

Kālanemi.note: The Purāṇa identifies Kamsa as the asura Kālanemi reborn.

Kālanābha.note: Some variable Purāṇic genealogical compilations list Kālanābha as his son.

Kālarātrī.note: Later theology assimilates Rātrī to Kālarātrī, though the Vedas contain no meeting or identity claim.

Kāliya.note: Garuḍa attacks Kāliya after the serpent refuses the tribute owed by snakes.
Krishna escapes Kāliya’s coils, dances upon his hoods, and spares him.
As Kṛṣṇa, Vishnu subdues the serpent Kāliya.
Kāliya poisons Yamunā’s waters until Kṛṣṇa subdues and expels him.

Kāmākhyā.note: Kāmākhyā’s sacred geography associates her region with Kāma’s recovery of bodily form.

Kāmākṣī.note: The major Kāñcīpuram goddess is theologically classified as Pārvatī.

Kāmāsura.note: As Vikata, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying desire.

Kārtavīrya Arjuna.note: Later accounts make the king’s desire for Kamadhenu central to the conflict.
Paraśurāma confronts Kārtavīrya after offenses against Jamadagni’s hermitage and miraculous cow.
Paraśurāma kills the Haihaya king with his axe and arrows.

Kātyāyanī.note: The goddess associated with Kātyāyana's hermitage fights Mahiṣa.
The Kātyāyanī manifestation kills Mahiṣa in this Purāṇic version.

Kāśyapa.note: Purāṇic systematization places Jatāyu in Kāśyapa’s lineage through Aruṇa.
Some post-Vedic Āditya genealogies make Kāśyapa the father of Tvaṣṭṛ.

Kēwān.note: Iranian Kēwān corresponds to Shani through the shared Saturnian planetary position.

Kṛta Yuga.note: Personified Kṛta appears in the allegorical retinue opposing Kali alongside Kalki.

Kṛttikās.note: The six or seven star goddesses nurse Skanda as collective foster-mothers.
The Kṛttikās and the larger Mother-host both participate in Skanda’s foster-mother complex.
Kṛttikās.source: Mahābhārata Skanda cycle and later Purāṇas

Kṛttikās.note: Pārvatī accepts or recovers the child fostered by the Kṛttikās.
The Kṛttikās nurse Śiva's multiply born son Skanda.
The Kṛttikās were wives of the Bears or Seven Sages before their separation.

Kṛśānu.note: Kṛśānu shoots at the bird carrying Soma and dislodges a feather.

Kṛśāśva.note: Daksha gives daughters to Kṛśāśva in the sixty-daughter genealogy.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa manifests as Viṣṇu among the Ādityas
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa declares Viṣṇu to be his manifestation within the Āditya collective.
Kṛṣṇa helps Agni burn Khāṇḍava and kills creatures attempting escape.
Kṛṣṇa identifies Airāvata as his supreme manifestation among lordly elephants.
Airāvata carries heavenly Gaṅgā water used by Indra to consecrate Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa declares Aryaman to be his exemplary manifestation among the Pitṛs.
Balarama is consistently presented as Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother.
Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva receive paired worship as divine Vṛṣṇi heroes.
Kṛṣṇa.source: Agathocles coins; Nāṇāghāṭ and Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions

Kṛṣṇa.note: The brothers herd cattle, play together, protect Vraja, and defeat demons.
Balarama and Kṛṣṇa defeat Kaṃsa’s wrestlers and overthrow his regime.
The brothers defeat Jarāsandha’s armies and protect the Yādavas.
Kṛṣṇa restrains Balarama when he moves against Bhīma for striking Duryodhana unfairly.
Brahmā removes Kṛṣṇa's cowherd boys and calves to test him.
Kṛṣṇa manifests every missing child and calf, bewildering Brahmā.
Overwhelmed by Kṛṣṇa's manifestations, Brahmā praises him and admits subordinate knowledge.
Brahmā appears in divine assemblies acknowledging Kṛṣṇa's supremacy.
Jayadeva praises Keśava appearing as Buddha to condemn animal slaughter.
Soma is the remote divine progenitor of Kṛṣṇa’s Yādava line.
She substitutes for infant Kṛṣṇa, enabling his survival from Kaṃsa.
Vaiṣṇava traditions identify the escaped goddess as Kṛṣṇa’s sister.
Pārvatī’s worship causes Kṛṣṇa to appear as Gaṇeśa.
Some versions link Gaṇeśa’s lunar curse with Kṛṣṇa’s false accusation.
Garuḍa carries Kṛṣṇa and serves as his Vaiṣṇava vehicle or banner.
Hanuman is associated with Kṛṣṇa through his presence on Arjuna’s banner.
Kṛṣṇa arbitrates the later bridge-building contest between Hanuman and Arjuna.
Indra sends catastrophic rain, but Kṛṣṇa lifts Govardhana and defeats his purpose.
After Govardhana, Indra joins Surabhi in honoring Kṛṣṇa as Govinda.
Indra resists when Kṛṣṇa removes the heavenly Pārijāta tree.
Mainstream Vaiṣṇava and Gaudiya traditions identify Jagannath as Kṛṣṇa.
Jagannath's hidden substance derives from Kṛṣṇa's unburned heart, navel, bones, body, or brahma.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa lists devotees who attained him
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa retrospectively names Jatāyu among those who attained him.
Bengali songs and images sometimes identify Kālī and Kṛṣṇa as the same dark absolute.
Kāma reappears as Pradyumna, the son of Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa declares himself kāmadhuk, the wish-yielding cow among cattle.
Surabhi praises Kṛṣṇa and bathes him with milk during his consecration.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa manifests Surabhi from his left side
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa produces Surabhi from his body in Goloka and first worships her.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kamsa’s plots against the prophesied child
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kamsa repeatedly engineers Kṛṣṇa’s death before confronting him in the arena.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Death of Kamsa in the arena
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa seizes Kamsa, throws him from the platform, and kills him.
Kamsa is Kṛṣṇa’s maternal uncle in the dominant narrative tradition.
Child Kṛṣṇa frees Kubera’s sons from their enchanted tree forms.
As Rukmiṇī, Lakṣmī accompanies and marries Viṣṇu’s incarnation Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa escapes Kāliya's coils, dances on his hoods, and expels him.
Kṛṣṇa spares Kāliya and grants protective footprints after the Nāginīs plead.
Nārada visits and praises Kṛṣṇa, reveals dangers, and provokes consequential events.
Kṛṣṇa names Nārada as his foremost manifestation among divine seers.
Paraśurāma embraces Kṛṣṇa and supports truthful counsel during the peace embassy.
Later narratives make Paraśurāma guide Kṛṣṇa’s campaign against Śṛgāla Vāsudeva.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Umā supports boons granted to Kṛṣṇa
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa beholds the divine couple, and Umā independently grants or supports blessings.
Kṛṣṇa descends in response to Earth's complaint and defeats oppressive rulers.
Kṛṣṇa directs the strategy using Ghaṭotkaca to exhaust Karṇa's divine missile.
Kṛṣṇa recognizes or receives Rati and the returned Pradyumna at Dvārakā.
Kṛṣṇa’s household receives Māyāvatī-Rati with his recovered son Pradyumna.
Śiva grants boons to Kṛṣṇa after his austerities.
Sectarian texts alternately depict Śiva and Kṛṣṇa subordinating or worshipping one another.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa names Śaṅkara among the Rudras
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa declares himself Śaṅkara among the Rudras.
The Rudras behold or are contained within Kṛṣṇa’s universal form.
Kṛṣṇa declares that the earlier seven great sages were born from his mind.
Sarasvatī emerges within Kṛṣṇa’s supreme Prakṛti and is assigned to Brahmā.
Sarasvatī praises Kṛṣṇa within the Purāṇa’s Kṛṣṇa-centered cosmology.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa declares himself Ananta among nāgas
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa includes Ananta among his pre-eminent divine manifestations.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Śeṣa descends as Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother
Kṛṣṇa.note: As Balarāma, Śeṣa becomes Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother and attendant expansion.
Śiva grants boons to Kṛṣṇa after receiving his worship.
Śiva fights Kṛṣṇa while defending his devotee Bāṇa.
Śiva and Kṛṣṇa reconcile after their battle over Bāṇa.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Kṛṣṇa urges Skanda to strike Tāraka
Kṛṣṇa.note: A late recension has Kṛṣṇa urge hesitant Skanda to use the śakti against Tāraka.
Kṛṣṇa wears fragrant tulsi garlands and receives its leaves in devotional offerings.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Gopīs question Tulasi while seeking Kṛṣṇa
Kṛṣṇa.note: The gopīs address the sacred plant while searching for the absent Kṛṣṇa.
Gauḍīya Vṛndādevī presides over the forest and arranges Kṛṣṇa’s meetings with Rādhā.
Regional Tulsi Vivah rites sometimes represent Kṛṣṇa as the sacred plant’s bridegroom.
Varuṇa supplies equipment used by Kṛṣṇa at Khāṇḍava, with weapon assignments varying by version.
Varuṇa worships Kṛṣṇa, acknowledges his supremacy, and returns the seized Nanda.
Kṛṣṇa declares himself Vāsuki among serpents.
The Vasus appear as manifestations contained within Kṛṣṇa's universal body.
Vāyu serves Kṛṣṇa through his second descent, Bhīma.
Viśvakarman constructs fortified Dvārakā for Kṛṣṇa and his people.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: God stands at Pandharpur for Pundalik
Kṛṣṇa.note: Vārkarī tradition identifies Vithoba as Kṛṣṇa standing for Pundalik.

Kṣema.note: Kṣema is named as one of Gaṇeśa’s sons.

Lalitā.note: Some Śrīvidyā systems equate the autonomous tantric supreme Goddess with Pārvatī.

Lalitā.myth: Lalitā organizes Radha and Krishna’s secret meetings
Lalitā.note: Radha’s principal sakhī mediates, defends her, and arranges meetings.
Lalitā compassionately restores Rati’s husband to embodied life with her glance.
Sarasvatī is emanated, empowered, or assigned a place within Lalitā’s court.

Lalitā Tripurasundarī.myth: Revelation of Lalitā’s deeds and names
Lalitā Tripurasundarī.note: Hayagrīva narrates Lalitā’s deeds and transmits her thousand names at her command.

Lava.note: Lava is a son of Rāma and Sītā.
Sītā gives birth to Lava during exile at Vālmīki’s hermitage.

Laṅkinī.note: Hanuman defeats Laṅkā’s guardian, who recognizes the city’s prophesied destruction.

Lobhāsura.note: As Gajavaktra or Gajānana, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying greed.

Lābha.note: Lābha is named as one of Gaṇeśa’s sons.

Madana.note: Bagalāmukhī neutralizes the demon’s speech-siddhi by grasping his tongue.
Before Bagalāmukhī kills him, Madana gains depiction or worship beside her.

Madhu.note: Threatened by Madhu, Brahmā invokes Mahāmāyā so Viṣṇu awakens and kills him.
She awakens Viṣṇu, enabling him to fight and kill Madhu.
Horse-headed Nārāyaṇa kills Madhu after recovering the Vedas.
Her withdrawal awakens Viṣṇu, indirectly enabling Madhu’s defeat and death.

Madhu.myth: Madhu threatens the Anantaśayana creation scene
Madhu.note: Madhu threatens Brahmā or confronts divine weapons beneath Viṣṇu and Śeṣa.
Vishnu kills the primordial-water demon Madhu alongside Kaiṭabha.

Madhva.note: Dvaita tradition identifies Madhva as Vāyu’s third incarnation and teacher of Vedānta.

Madāsura.note: As Ekadanta, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying intoxicated pride.

Mahirāvaṇa.note: Hanuman assumes five faces, extinguishes directional lamps, and kills the underworld demon.

Mahiṣa.myth: Skanda defeats Tāraka and Mahiṣa among the asuras
Mahiṣa.note: Tāraka and Mahiṣa appear as separate asuras defeated by Skanda; no kinship is stated.

Mahiṣi.note: Ayyappa battles the buffalo demoness whom ordinary gods and men cannot defeat.
Ayyappa kills Mahiṣi, sometimes releasing a cursed celestial woman.

Mahākāla.note: Hindu traditions sometimes identify Bhairava with Mahākāla.
Vajrayāna images show Gaṇeśa or Vināyaka trampled and subordinated.
Tantric systems pair Kālī with Mahākāla as his feminine power and equivalent of time.
Nandin and Mahākāla are paired as armed guardians of Śiva’s doorway.
Yama appears with Mahākāla and other dharmapālas in protector cycles.

Mahālakṣmī.note: Some regional systems absorb the Mothers into Mahālakṣmī or add her to their group.
Mahāsarasvatī and Mahālakṣmī are coordinated manifestations of the supreme Goddess.

Mahāmāyā.note: Śākta systematization assimilates Rātrī into Mahāmāyā, the universal power of manifestation and concealment.
Śākta texts identify Satī as the supreme Goddess voluntarily embodied.

Mahānābha.note: Some variable Purāṇic genealogical compilations list Mahānābha as his son.

Mahāsena.myth: Three divine youths appear together on coinage
Mahāsena.note: Kushan coinage presents Mahāsena alongside Skanda-Kumāra and Viśākha.
Later consolidation treats Mahāsena as a name or form of Skanda.

Mahāvairocana.note: Paired Kangiten is ritually situated within Mahāvairocana’s esoteric mandalic order.

Mahāvīra.note: Śakra carries the newborn Mahāvīra to Meru and performs or directs his bath.
Śakra receives Mahāvīra’s hair and attends significant events and preaching.

Mahāśvetā.note: A stray secondary tradition names Mahāśvetā as Sampāti’s mother.

Mahīṣī.note: Later Ayyappa traditions identify the buffalo-demoness Mahīṣī as Mahiṣāsura's sister.

Maināka.note: Maināka offers Hanuman rest; Hanuman politely touches the mountain and continues.
Developed genealogies call her the sister of the mountain Maināka.

Makha.note: The twins act as ritual surgeons and restore the severed head of personified Sacrifice.

Mallinātha.note: Some Jain lists assign Kubera as Mallinātha’s yaksha attendant.

Mamatā.note: Bṛhaspati coerces his pregnant sister-in-law despite her explicit protest.

Mamāsura.note: As Vighnarāja, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying possessiveness.

Manasvin.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Manasvin.note: Manasvin and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Manasā.note: Dhanvantari and his disciples oppose the snake goddess’s poisonous and magical power.
Eastern Indian traditions frequently call Manasā Vāsuki’s sister.

Mandara.myth: Kūrma supports the rotating churning mountain
Mandara.note: Kūrma bears Mandara when the mountain lacks a stable base.
Mandara serves as the churning staff when Uchchaihshravas emerges.

Mandodarī.note: A Jain variant makes Mandodarī and Rāvaṇa Sītā’s biological parents.
Sītā is generated through Mandodarī’s ingestion of sages’ blood.
