Mandā.note: Recent devotional accounts inconsistently name Mandā as Shani’s wife.

Manu Vaivasvata.note: Through Vivasvat, the Āditya lineage becomes ancestral to Manu Vaivasvata.
As another son of Vivasvant, Manu is their brother or half-brother.
Manu is Yama’s sibling or half-sibling depending on the recension.

Maru.note: The immortal Maru resumes Solar dynastic authority under Kalki’s restored order.

Marīci.note: Marīci is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Marīci is Hiranyakashipu’s grandfather in many Purāṇic cosmologies.
Marīci is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.

Matsarāsura.note: As Vakratuṇḍa, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying envy.

Maya.note: Community genealogies name Maya among Viśvakarman's five artisan sons.

Maya Dānava.note: Agni’s conflagration threatens Maya, who survives through Arjuna’s protection.

Mañjuśrī.note: Buddhist Vajrabhairava is classified as a wrathful form of Mañjuśrī, not Hindu Bhairava.
In tantric tradition, Mañjuśrī manifests as Yamāntaka to overcome Yama.

Maṇavāḷa Māmunikaḷ.note: Certain lineage traditions identify Maṇavāḷa Māmunikaḷ with Śeṣa’s continuing incarnational service.

Maṇigrīva.note: Maṇigrīva is Kubera’s son and Nalakūvara’s brother.

Maṇimat.note: Maṇimat is Kubera’s yakṣa associate whose curse-ordained death Kubera explains.

Meghamāla.note: Meghamāla is named as a child of Kalki and Ramā.

Meghamālin.note: Dharaṇendra counters Meghamālin's supernatural storm while protecting Pārśvanātha.

Meghanāda.note: Meghanāda defeats and binds Indra, earning the title Indrajit after negotiations.
Indra is released after Brahmā intervenes and rewards his captor.
Meghanāda, later named Indrajit, is Ravana’s best-attested son.

Meher Baba.note: Followers sometimes interpret Meher Baba’s universal Avatar status through Kalki imagery.

Mekhalā.note: Buddhist traditions associate Chinnamuṇḍā’s self-decapitation imagery with the adept Mekhalā.

Menakā.note: Viśvāvasu’s sexual union with Menakā produces Pramadvarā.
Indra sends Menakā to disrupt austerities threatening his celestial position.

Menā.note: As Pārvatī, Annapūrṇā inherits Menā as her mother.
As Pārvatī, Durgā is treated as Menā’s daughter.
Ganga is the daughter of Menā and Himavat.
She is the younger daughter of Menā and Himavat.
The sages console Menā and help secure her acceptance of Śiva as bridegroom.
After abandoning Satī’s body, the Goddess is born from Menā.

Milk Ocean.note: Epic and Purāṇic accounts make Lakṣmī the ocean’s daughter or product.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad.note: Ahmadi publications present Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as fulfilling Hindu expectations including Kalki.

Miθra.note: Miθra is Mitra's secure Iranian cognate but developed as a historically distinct deity.

Mohinī.note: After demons seize Dhanvantari’s jar, Mohinī recovers and distributes its nectar to the gods.

Mohinī.myth: Mohinī distributes nectar during the asura’s infiltration
Mohinī.note: Ketu participates only retroactively as the future severed body of the infiltrator.

Mohinī.myth: Sequential manifestations in the nectar restoration
Mohinī.note: Kūrma and Mohinī are consecutive forms of Viṣṇu, not independent beings meeting.
Rāhu enters Mohinī’s divine company in disguise and receives nectar before detection.
Śiva becomes desirous upon seeing Viṣṇu’s female form Mohinī.
Mohinī is the enchanting female form assumed by Vishnu.

Mohāsura.note: As Mahodara, Gaṇeśa defeats the demon embodying delusion.

Mount Meru.myth: Vāyu assaults and breaks a mountain peak
Mount Meru.note: Epic and Purāṇic variants describe Vāyu breaking or moving peaks with his force.

Muni.note: Several traditions derive the Mauneya Gandharvas from Kaśyapa and Muni.

Murukaṉ.note: Local tradition associates Jatāyu and Murukaṉ as fellow worshippers of Śiva.

Muḥammad.note: Modern Muslim apologetic writings identify Muḥammad with Kalki through selective name and biography comparisons.

Muṇḍa.note: Durgā’s wrath produces Kālī, who attacks and kills Muṇḍa.
Kālī battles Muṇḍa before killing him.
Kālī kills Muṇḍa and carries his head to Caṇḍikā.

Muṇḍa.myth: Report and attempted capture of the Goddess
Muṇḍa.note: Muṇḍa reports the Goddess’s beauty, then is ordered by Śumbha to capture her.

Muṣṭika.note: Balarama defeats and commonly kills Kaṃsa’s wrestler Muṣṭika.
Kamsa’s champion fights Balarāma and is killed by him.

Mā Maṅgalā.note: Petitioned by Jagannath's search party, she reveals the sacred trees' locations through dreams.

Māheśvarī.note: Māheśvarī combats the blood-born Andhakas and drinks their blood.
Kālī and Māheśvarī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.
She struck him with her trident.
Māheśvarī fights the brothers’ army in Śiva’s form and insignia.

Mālikappurattamma.note: She requests marriage; Ayyappa postpones it until first-time pilgrims cease arriving.

Māra.note: In Baka's episode, Māra supports the deluded Brahmā and tries intimidating the Buddha.
Buddhist sources sometimes call the sensual tempter Māra Kāmadeva or Kāmamāra.

Māriṣā.note: Māriṣā develops from Pramlocā’s child or embryonic material left among trees.
Māriṣā bears the reborn Daksha to the ten Pracetas.

Mārkaṇḍeya.note: Śiva saves his devotee by defeating or checking Yama.
Śiva protects the boy devotee Mārkaṇḍeya from Death.
Mārkaṇḍeya encounters Nārāyaṇa and sees the cosmos within the divine child.

Mārtāṇḍa.note: Aditi casts away Mārtāṇḍa after approaching the gods with seven sons.

Mārtāṇḍa.myth: Mārtāṇḍa restored for birth and death
Mārtāṇḍa.note: Aditi brings her rejected son back for recurring birth and death.

Mārtāṇḍa.myth: Malformed eighth son reshaped by his brothers
Mārtāṇḍa.note: Aditi's malformed eighth child is reshaped by the Ādityas.
Mārtāṇḍa is Aditi’s eighth son, distinguished from seven accepted Ādityas.
Mārtāṇḍa is excluded from the seven, then restored for recurring birth and death.

Mārīca.note: Mārīca imitates Rama’s voice, prompting Sita to send Lakshmana away.
Mārīca lures Rāma away by assuming the form of a golden deer.
Rāma mortally shoots Mārīca while pursuing the golden deer.
Ravana threatens Mārīca into becoming the golden deer used to isolate Sītā.
Disguised as a golden deer, Mārīca draws Sītā’s protectors away.

Mātali.note: Mātali drives Sakka’s chariot and counsels him about moral conduct.

Mātariśvan.note: Mātariśvan brings Agni from afar or reveals him from concealment.
Mātariśvan gives or conveys the divine fire Agni to Manu.

Mātṛkā.note: Mātṛkā is named as Aryaman’s wife in a Purāṇic genealogy.

Māyā-Sītā.note: Agni substitutes Māyā-Sītā for the concealed real Sītā and later reverses the exchange.
An illusory double replaces Sītā during abduction and is exchanged at the fire.

Māṇik Prabhu.note: Later communities identify Māṇik Prabhu as a manifestation of Dattātreya.

Mīnalinī.note: Mīnalinī appears as Kubera’s child in later genealogical lists.

Mīnākṣī.note: Madurai’s autonomous sovereign goddess is later identified with Pārvatī.

Mūṣika.note: Gaṇeśa subdues the destructive mouse-being with his noose.
The defeated being receives mercy and becomes Gaṇeśa’s mount.

Mṛtyu.note: Brahmā creates personified Death to destroy living beings.
Brahmā persuades or commands the initially reluctant Death to perform her duty.
Prajāpati uses sacrifice and knowledge to evade or overcome Death's threat.
Mṛtyu is sometimes Yama and sometimes a distinct death power or female personification.

Nabhāga.note: Nabhāga appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Nahusha.note: Bṛhaspati resists Nahusha’s claim over Indrāṇī principally through counsel and strategy.
After Nahusha forces sages to carry him and assaults Agastya, their curse causes his fall.
Nahusha coerces a variably constituted group of great sages into carrying his palanquin.

Nahuṣa.note: Nahuṣa replaces the hidden Indra and threatens Śacī before his cursed fall.

Nakula.note: Mādrī invokes the pair and bears Nakula as their divine son.
Nakula ignores the yaksha’s warning, drinks from the lake, and falls apparently dead.
The yaksha restores Nakula after Yudhiṣṭhira chooses him for revival.

Nala.note: Nala directs construction of the causeway carrying Rāma’s army to Laṅkā.
Nala is Viśvakarman's son and inherits his engineering ability.

Nalakūbara.note: Rambhā is Nalakūbara’s intended partner or wife and reports Rāvaṇa’s assault to him.
Nalakūbara curses Ravana’s head to split if he forces another unwilling woman.

Namuci.note: The twins enter the medical aftermath of Indra's adversarial encounter with Namuci.
Indra is celebrated as the killer of Namuci in early hymns.
Indra circumvents their pact by killing Namuci with foam at twilight.

Nanda.note: Nanda joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.
As Kṛṣṇa, Jagannath is the foster son of Nanda.
Nanda raises Krishna as his foster-son in Vraja.
Nanda fights or restrains Bali’s Asura forces as Vāmana’s attendant.

Nanda.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Nanda.note: Nanda and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Nandinī.note: As Vasu Dyu, he abducts Nandinī at his wife's request.
Surabhi is Nandinī’s mother through Kaśyapa.
Later retellings merge Nandinī with Kamadhenu despite their distinct epic genealogy.
Dyu steals Nandinī and her calf with aid from the other Vasus.

Nandā.myth: Nandā kills Mahiṣa in the Vindhyas
Nandā.note: Regional Purāṇic versions assign Mahiṣa's death to Nandā.

Nappiṉṉai.note: Later traditions equate Radha with Krishna’s Tamil cowherd beloved Nappiṉṉai.

Nara.note: Rāhu and Nara appear in the same churning battle without an independent encounter.
Some Mahābhārata manuscript traditions invoke Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and Sarasvatī before recitation.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa perform austerities together as a paired sage formation.

Naraka.note: Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa fights Naraka in the expanded Kṛṣṇa narrative cycle.

Nariṣyanta.note: Nariṣyanta appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Narāntaka.note: Narāntaka is named among Ravana’s sons.

Nemi.note: Nemi serves as a commander whom Bali orders to stop fighting.

Neminātha.note: Gaṇeśa appears as a subordinate attendant in some ensembles associated with Neminātha.
Jain universal history treats Krishna and Neminātha as cousins.
Gomedha and Ambikā are assigned as Neminātha’s attendant pair in prominent Jain traditions.

Nidrā.note: Lakshmana asks Nidrā to leave him, and she transfers his sleep to Urmilā.

Nikṣubhā.note: Nikṣubhā appears as an additional or alternative wife in particular later lists.

Nirṛti.note: Nirṛti joins the directional gods who bless Narasimha’s Ahobilam wedding.
Rākṣasas are associated with Nirṛti, destructive disorder, and the southwest.

Nisunda.note: Niśumbha is generated from Nisunda following Nisunda’s fatal encounter with Tilottamā.

Nityānanda.note: Gaudīya theology identifies Nityānanda as Balarama’s Kali-age manifestation.

Niśaṭha.note: Niśaṭha is commonly listed as a child of Balarama and Revatī.

Niśākara.note: Niśākara prevents the wingless Sampāti from killing himself.
Niśākara foretells Sampāti’s future service to Rāma and the arrival of Sītā’s searchers.
Niśākara’s fulfilled prediction or ascetic power is associated with Sampāti’s restored wings.

Nābhāganediṣṭha.note: Nābhāganediṣṭha is Manu’s son, with traditions varying over his name and inheritance.

Nāga weapon-serpents.note: Indrajit’s supernatural serpent weapon binds and disables Lakshmana and Rama.

Nārāyaṇa.note: In one variant, Nārāyaṇa is the disguised carpenter who makes Jagannath's unfinished body.
Some Mahābhārata manuscript traditions invoke Nārāyaṇa, Nara, and Sarasvatī before recitation.

Nīlamādhava.note: The vanished forest deity precedes Jagannath's manifestation through the miraculous sacred log.

Nīlā.note: Recent devotional accounts inconsistently name Nīlā as Shani’s wife.

Nīlādevī.note: Nīlādevī joins Lakṣmī as another consort or feminine divine form.
Nīlādevī and Bhūdevī are co-consorts of Viṣṇu in some South Indian triads.
Developed South Indian traditions place Nīlādevī beside Vishnu, though her status varies.

Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī.note: Datta tradition presents Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī as a successive manifestation of Dattātreya.

Ocean.note: Personified Ocean receives the thousand-headed serpent returning from Balarāma.
Later reception increasingly identifies the personified Ocean confronted by Rāma with Varuṇa.

Other seven Vasus.note: The seven Vasus assist Dyu's theft and share his curse.

Oēšo.note: Kushan Oēšo combines an Iranian name with major Śaiva visual attributes.

Padmasambhava.note: Nyingma histories and treasure texts associate Padmasambhava with Hayagrīva practice and transmission.

Padmavati.note: Oneness devotees treated Padmavati as divine consort to Vijaykumar Naidu’s modern Kalki persona.

Padubāī.myth: Pastoral traditions of Viṭṭhal and Padubāī
Padubāī.note: Dhangar traditions link Viṭṭhal and Padubāī within a proposed older pastoral cult.
Padubāī.source: Dhere, Rise of a Folk God

Pampa.note: Hampi’s local goddess is incorporated into Śaivism as Pārvatī.

Parjanya.note: Parjanya is called a son of Heaven.

Parvata.note: Nārada and Parvata are paired as possessors of sacrificial knowledge.
Received tradition jointly assigns Soma hymns to Nārada Kāṇva and Parvata Kāṇva.
Later tales make the companion sages rivals over marriage.

Parā.myth: Trika’s triadic manifestation of divine power
Parā.note: Parā expresses one aspect of Bhairava’s triadic power.

Parāparā.myth: Trika’s triadic manifestation of divine power
Parāparā.note: Parāparā expresses one aspect of Bhairava’s triadic power.

Parāvatas.note: The Vedic Sarasvatī overcomes the Parāvatas as a martial protector.

Patañjali.myth: Śeṣa incarnates as the sage Patañjali
Patañjali.note: Medieval Chidambaram tradition makes Patañjali a serpent manifestation of Śeṣa.

Pavamāna.note: Some Purāṇic genealogies name Pavamāna among Agni’s progeny.

Pañcasikha.note: Pañcasikha sings before the Buddha and secures Sakka’s audience.

Pañcika.note: Some Buddhist contexts assimilate Pañcika iconographically and functionally to Kubera or Jambhala.

Paśu.note: Paśu is genealogized as Savitr and Pṛśni’s son.

Paṇis.note: The Vedic Sarasvatī defeats the Paṇis while protecting and enriching her peoples.

Pippala.note: Late genealogical catalogues list Pippala among Mitra's children.

Pipru.note: Indra defeats Pipru among the enemies named in victory hymns.

Pitṛs.note: Daksha gives Svadhā to the ancestral Pitṛs as wife or mediator.

Prabala.note: Prabala joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Prabhā.note: Prabhā appears as an additional or alternative wife in particular later lists.

Prabhāsa.note: Later Vasu lists substitute Prabhāsa for Dyu in Bhīṣma's divine prehistory.
Viśvakarman is born as the son of the Vasu Prabhāsa.

Pradyumna.note: Saṃkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna belong to the Vṛṣṇi hero group and four-vyūha system.
The Kāma burned by Rudra is born again as Pradyumna.
Pradyumna is an important son of Krishna.
As Māyāvatī, Rati raises the rescued Pradyumna in Śambara’s household.
Rati reveals Pradyumna’s identity and teaches him superior magical knowledge.
Rati reunites conjugally with Pradyumna after recognizing Kāma’s rebirth.
Rati accompanies Pradyumna home and is received as his wife.
The thousand-headed Ananta serves Pradyumna as his charioteer.
Pradyumna is a son of Vishnu in his Kṛṣṇa manifestation.
Pradyumna is a member of the fourfold emanational sequence derived from Vāsudeva.
Vithoba inherits Kṛṣṇa’s son through identification with Kṛṣṇa.

Prahlāda.note: Prahlāda warns Andhaka not to covet Pārvatī or attack Tryambaka.
Bali is Prahlāda’s grandson through Virocana.
Prahlāda praises Bali’s surrender and intercedes after Vāmana binds him.
Prahlāda is Hiranyakashipu’s devoted son and eventual dynastic successor.
He subjects Prahlāda to weapons, poison, snakes, elephants, fire, falling, and drowning.
In a martial variant, Prahlāda initially joins his brothers resisting Narasiṃha.
After the killing, Prahlāda requests purification and forgiveness for his father.
Nārada teaches devotion that the unborn Prahlāda hears and remembers.
Narasimha vindicates Prahlāda’s devotion and ends his father’s persecution.
Narasimha blesses Prahlāda, grants boons, and installs him as ruler.
Prahlāda approaches the raging deity, prays, and successfully calms him.
Śukra serves the Daitya order of Prahlāda; some texts place them together.
The Gaveṣṭhin genealogy makes the brothers descendants of Prahlāda.

Prahlāda.myth: Prahlāda allegedly gives the horse to Bali
Prahlāda.note: Modern devotional retellings claim Prahlāda owned Uchchaihshravas and gave him to Bali.

Prahlāda.myth: Prahlāda praises Vāmana after Bali’s binding
Prahlāda.note: Prahlāda praises Vāmana and participates in Bali’s settlement in Sutala.
Vishnu manifests as Narasiṃha to protect his devotee Prahlāda from Hiraṇyakaśipu.

Pralamba.note: Balarama kills the disguised demon with a blow to the head.
Pralamba is affiliated with Kamsa’s demonic forces and killed by Balarāma.
Krishna participates in the cowherd games infiltrated by Pralamba, whom Balarāma kills.

Pramadvarā.note: Menakā and Viśvāvasu are the parents of Pramadvarā.
The Gandharva Viśvāvasu fathers Pramadvarā with Menakā.

Prasūti.note: Prasūti is wife of the Brahmā-born Daksha and bears his daughters.
Prasūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.
Prasūti is Satī’s mother in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Pratyaṅgirā.note: The lion-faced goddess intervenes to quell Narasimha’s escalating conflict with Śarabha.

Priyavrata.note: Priyavrata is commonly listed as a child of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.

Prājña.note: Prājña is named as one of Kalki’s brothers.

Prāṃśu.note: Some Purāṇic lists name Prāṃśu as one of Vaivasvata Manu’s sons.

Prāṇa.note: Later systems correlate Vāyu with vital breath; Madhva identifies Mukhya-prāṇa as the conscious deity Vāyu.

Prīti.note: Some iconographic and regional traditions present Prīti as Kāma’s second consort.
Rati and Prīti appear together as personifications associated with Kāma.
Rati and Prīti jointly respond to Kāma’s flower arrows.

Pulaha.note: Pulaha is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Pulaha is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.

Pulastya.note: Pulastya is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
Some Mahābhārata passages make Kubera the son or quasi-son of Pulastya.
The dominant genealogy makes Pulastya Kubera’s grandfather through Viśravas.
Pulastya is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.
Ravana is the grandson of Brahmā’s mind-born son Pulastya.
Some Purāṇic genealogical variants derive the yakshas through Pulastya.

Puloman.note: The demon Puloman questions Agni, whose truthful answer enables Pulomā’s abduction.
Some accounts say Indra kills Puloman, father of his consort Pulomajā.

Pulomā.note: Some traditions make Bhṛgu’s wife Pulomā the mother of Śukra.

Purandhi.note: Purandhi and Aryaman jointly give the bride for household governance.
Purandhi and Bhaga help give the bride household authority.

Puruṣa.note: A later genealogy makes Agni a son or emanation of cosmic Puruṣa or Virāj.
Lakṣmī and Śrī are separately named as Puruṣa’s two wives.
Later exegesis closely relates Puruṣa to Prajāpati, though early texts do not consistently identify them.

Puruṣa.myth: Vāyu emerges from the cosmic Person’s breath
Puruṣa.note: Vāyu or wind arises from Puruṣa’s breath in a late Vedic cosmogony.

Purūravas.note: Urvaśī shares a conditional union with Purūravas, followed by separation and intermittent reunion.
Urvaśī leaves after a breached nudity taboo, then grants Purūravas limited reunions.
Purūravas rescues Urvaśī after a demon abducts her.
Budha fathers Purūravas with Ilā and receives the newborn.
Soma is Purūravas’s divine ancestor through Budha and Ilā.
Manu is Purūravas’s ancestor through Manu’s child Ilā and Ilā’s union with Budha.

Puṣkalā.note: Regional Tamil Śāstā and Aiyaṉār forms portray Puṣkalā as his consort.

Puṣkara.note: Epic or Purāṇic genealogical lists name Puṣkara among Varuṇa’s sons.

Puṣpadanta.note: Puṣpadanta joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Pārśvanātha.note: Pārśva saves serpents trapped inside an ascetic's burning log.
Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī shelter the meditating Pārśva from Meghamālin's storm.
Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī shelter or attend Pārśvanātha and are later classified as his yaksha and yakshi.

Pāvaka.note: Some Purāṇic genealogies name Pāvaka among Agni’s progeny.

Pūrṇā.note: Regional Tamil Śāstā and Aiyaṉār forms portray Pūrṇā as his consort.

Pūtanā.myth: Attempt to poison the infant Kṛṣṇa
Pūtanā.note: The child-killing demoness advances Kamsa’s program by offering Kṛṣṇa poisoned milk.
Krishna kills the poison-bearing demoness by suckling and later grants her salvation.
As the infant Kṛṣṇa, Vishnu defeats the murderous being Pūtanā.

Pṛthivī.note: Brāhmaṇa ritual theology explicitly identifies Aditi with earth and foundation.

Pṛthivī.myth: Heaven and Earth as universal parents
Pṛthivī.note: Paired with Pṛthivī as cosmic parents who generate and sustain beings.

Pṛthivī.myth: Protection and longevity of a child
Pṛthivī.note: Father Heaven and Mother Earth jointly protect a boy and grant longevity.

Pṛthivī.myth: Umā curses Earth after the gods interrupt her union
Pṛthivī.note: She curses Earth to have many husbands after interruption of her union.

Pṛthivī.myth: Śeṣa enters below and bears the earth
Pṛthivī.note: Śeṣa physically supports and stabilizes the personified earth.

Pṛthu.note: Later summaries say Pṛthu appoints Airāvata king of elephants; the primary locus is uncertain.
Pṛthu pursues Earth and threatens her with an arrow after she withholds crops.
Earth negotiates with Pṛthu and yields seeds and food after he levels the land.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa figuratively makes Earth Pṛthu's daughter and derives her name from him.

Pṛśni.note: Pṛśni bears or mothers the Maruts as their cow-like dappled maternal figure.
As mother of the Maruts, she is Rudra's implied poetic partner.
Pṛśni is mother of the Maruts, who are also called Rudras.
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa names Pṛśni as Savitr’s wife.

Pṛṣadhra.note: Pṛṣadhra appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Rakṣases.note: Agni is invoked to burn, pierce and expel Rakṣases and hostile sorcery.

Rambha.note: Mahiṣa is born as Rambha's shape-changing buffalo son.
Mahiṣa emerges through Rambha's union and the buffalo-mother's funeral-pyre death.

Rambhā.note: Tumburu’s neglect or attachment involving Rambhā contributes to Kubera’s curse.
Indra sends Rambhā to disrupt austerities threatening his celestial position.
Ravana sexually assaults Rambhā, prompting Nalakūbara’s punitive curse.

Rambhāsura.myth: Rambha’s rebirth from the funeral pyre
Rambhāsura.note: A modern encyclopedic synthesis identifies Raktabīja as Rambhāsura reborn.

Ratnasambhava.note: Tibetan tantric systems treat yellow Jambhala as an emanation of Ratnasambhava.

Rauhiṇa.note: Indra defeats Rauhiṇa among his named Rigvedic adversaries.

Raṅgadevī.myth: Raṅgadevī coordinates Radha’s adornment and secret meetings
Raṅgadevī.note: She assists Radha with dress, messages, reconciliation, and rendezvous.

Revanta.note: Many Purāṇic accounts make the horse-riding Revanta a son of Sūrya and Saṃjñā.
Uchchaihshravas carries Revanta into Viṣṇu’s presence.
Several later genealogies place Revanta in Yamī’s solar family, though his maternity varies.
Later solar genealogy makes Revanta Yamuna's half-sibling through transformed Saṃjñā.

Revati.note: Systematic avatāra lists occasionally assign Revati as a corresponding Lakṣmī form.

Revatī.note: Balarama marries Revatī after cosmic time has erased her original generation.
Later accounts say Balarama shortens Revatī’s archaic gigantic body with his plough.
Late genealogical catalogues name Revatī as Mitra's wife, though readings require verification.

Revaṇta.note: Some Purāṇas make the horse-associated solar son Revaṇta their brother.

Reṇukā.note: Reṇukā is Paraśurāma’s mother and is commonly described as royally born.
At Jamadagni’s command, Paraśurāma cuts off his mother’s head.
He uses Jamadagni’s offered boon to restore Reṇukā without memory of her execution.

Riaz Ahmed Gohar Shahi.note: Supporters present Gohar Shahi as a universal messianic figure including Kalki.

Riddhi.note: Riddhi replaces or joins Buddhi as Gaṇeśa’s wife.

Rohiṇī.note: Rohiṇī receives the transferred embryo and gives birth to Balarama.
Secondary genealogical traditions name Rohiṇī rather than Tārā as Budha’s mother.
Rohiṇī is Chandra’s favored wife among Daksha’s lunar-station daughters.
Rohiṇī is one of Daksha’s twenty-seven lunar-mansion daughters.
Daksha gives Rohiṇī to Soma, whose preference for her provokes conflict.
Shani approaches or threatens to pierce Rohiṇī, portending a catastrophic drought.
Rohiṇī receives the transferred embryo and gives birth to Balarāma.

Rukmini.note: Rukmini is Vithoba’s principal consort in temple and regional traditions.

Rukmini.myth: Rukmini’s anger and withdrawal to Dindiravana
Rukmini.note: Rukmini withdraws angrily; Kṛṣṇa-Vithoba follows her toward Pandharpur.
Some variants have Rukmini accompany Kṛṣṇa when he visits Pundalik.

Rukmiṇī.note: Rukmiṇī is counted among Jagannath's consorts through his Kṛṣṇa identity.
Rukmiṇī gives birth to Kāma reborn as Pradyumna.
Krishna abducts Rukmiṇī at her request and marries her.
Vaiṣṇava tradition consistently identifies Kṛṣṇa’s wife Rukmiṇī with Lakṣmī.
Rati reveals Rukmiṇī as Pradyumna’s birth mother and becomes her daughter-in-law.

Rumaṇvān.note: Rumaṇvān is one of Paraśurāma’s elder brothers in the Vana Parvan.
Paraśurāma requests that Rumaṇvān recover from Jamadagni’s curse or stupefaction.

Rājñī.note: Rājñī appears as an additional or alternative wife in particular later lists.

Rāmānuja.note: Śrī Vaiṣṇava hagiography understands Rāmānuja as an incarnation of Ādiśeṣa.

Sadāśiva.note: The text assigns a Viṣṇu-form of Sadāśiva as Kamalā’s partner.

Sahadeva.note: Mādrī invokes the pair and bears Sahadeva as their divine son.
Sahadeva ignores the yaksha’s warning, drinks from the lake, and falls apparently dead.
The yaksha restores Sahadeva after Yudhiṣṭhira passes the test.

Sahasramukha Rāvaṇa.note: After he defeats Rāma, Sītā assumes a martial form and attacks him.
Sītā as Mahākālī destroys Sahasramukha Rāvaṇa and his army.

Sakka.note: In Buddhist tradition, Erāvana serves as Sakka’s marvelous elephant.
The Gandhabba Pañcasikha approaches the Buddha musically as Sakka’s emissary.

Samael Aun Weor.note: The modern Gnostic teacher adopted Kalki Avatar as an esoteric title.

Samudra.note: Vishnu directs and supports the churning of Samudra for amṛta.

Sanaka.note: Sanaka is one of Brahmā's four mind-born Kumāra sons.
Sanaka helps curse Jaya to take births away from Viṣṇu.

Sanandana.note: Sanandana is one of Brahmā's four mind-born Kumāra sons.
Sanandana helps curse Jaya to take births away from Viṣṇu.

Sanatkumāra.note: Sanatkumāra is one of Brahmā's four mind-born Kumāra sons.
Sanatkumāra helps curse Jaya to take births away from Viṣṇu.

Sanatkumāra.myth: Sanatkumāra teaches Nārada and is called Skanda
Sanatkumāra.note: The Upaniṣad explicitly identifies the teacher Sanatkumāra with Skanda.

Sanatkumāra.myth: Instruction in Śiva worship and yoga
Sanatkumāra.note: Sanatkumāra teaches Nandin Śiva worship and yoga.
Another tradition has Sanatkumāra punish Nandin and later release him.

Sanatkumāra.myth: Nārada’s ascent from learning to plenitude
Sanatkumāra.note: Sanatkumāra teaches the sorrowing Nārada knowledge of the Self and bhūman.

Sanatkumāras.note: Vishnu or his tradition transmits theological knowledge to the Sanatkumāras.

Sandhyā.note: Later accounts connect Sandhyā to Rati through death, purification, or rebirth.

Sanātana.note: Sanātana is one of Brahmā's four mind-born Kumāra sons.
Sanātana helps curse Jaya to take births away from Viṣṇu.

Sarama.note: Sarama locates the cattle whose recovery is associated with Indra and the Aṅgirases.

Saramā.myth: Guardians of the road to the dead
Saramā.note: Yama’s two four-eyed road-guarding dogs are described as Saramā’s offspring.

Sarayu.note: Lakshmana withdraws his senses at the river before divine translation.

Sarayū.note: Rāma enters the Sarayū and returns to his divine condition.

Saraṇyū.note: Saraṇyū bears the Aśvins within the compressed solar-family genealogy.
Later genealogies make Saraṇyū, also called Saṃjñā, the mother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Saraṇyū, later called Saṃjñā, is Sūrya’s chief wife.
Tvaṣṭṛ is Saraṇyū’s father and prepares her marriage to Vivasvat.
Later solar genealogies make Saraṇyū or Saṃjñā Yama’s mother.
Learned Vedic genealogy systematizes Saraṇyū as mother of Yamī and Yama.

Sarvavāhana.note: Some Jain traditions identify a Kubera-like yakṣa with Sarvavāhana.

Sarvānubhūti.note: Some Jain traditions identify a Kubera-like yakṣa with Sarvānubhūti, though usage is inconsistent.

Sarūpā.note: Sarūpā and Bhūta are parents of a separately enumerated Rudra group.

Satyabhāmā.note: Indra opposes Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā during their removal of the heavenly tree.
Satyabhāmā is counted among Jagannath's consorts through his Kṛṣṇa identity.
Satyabhāmā is one of Krishna’s principal queens.
Satyabhāmā often accompanies Krishna when he kills Narakāsura.
Some later traditions connect Satyabhāmā with a form of Lakṣmī.
Later sectarian retellings identify Satyabhāmā as Bhūdevī incarnate in the Naraka cycle.
Satyabhāmā appears as a subordinate or neighboring image in the temple complex.

Satyavatī.note: Satyavatī is Paraśurāma’s paternal grandmother in the dominant genealogy.

Saudharma Indra.note: Airāvata carries the Jain Indra during the newborn Tīrthaṅkara’s ceremonial cycle.

Saṃhlāda.note: Saṃhlāda is listed among Hiranyakashipu’s sons.

Saṃjñā.note: Mare-formed Saṃjñā conceives or bears the twins after Sūrya approaches as a stallion.
Saṃjñā creates Chāyā, whose substitution enables Shani’s birth into the solar family.
Unable to endure Sūrya’s brilliance, Saṃjñā leaves Chāyā as her substitute.
Sūrya finds mare-shaped Saṃjñā, becomes a stallion, and fathers divine children.
Purāṇic versions identify Saṃjñā as Viśvakarman's daughter.
He reduces Sūrya's radiance so Saṃjñā can endure her husband.
Purāṇic solar genealogies make Saṃjñā the mother of Yamī-Yamunā.
Purāṇic solar genealogies name Saṃjñā as Yamuna's mother.

Saṃkarṣaṇa.note: Poison-fire from Saṃkarṣaṇa’s mouth contributes to the dissolution preceding Matsya’s rescue.

Saṃvarta.note: Saṃvarta appears as Bṛhaspati’s brother in epic Aṅgirasa genealogies.

Saṅkarṣaṇa.note: Pāñcarātra and Purāṇic systems identify or closely coordinate Ananta with Saṅkarṣaṇa.

Seven Gods of Fortune.note: Benzaiten joins the fortune-god ensemble as its sole commonly female member.

Shirdi Sai Baba.note: Some modern Datta organizations incorporate Shirdi Sai Baba into Dattātreya incarnation lists.

Siddhi.note: Gaṇeśa marries Siddhi after defeating Skanda in the race.

Sindūra.note: Gaṇeśa kills the demon, explaining vermilion worship or his red coloration.

Siṃhamukha.note: Murukaṉ defeats Siṃhamukha during the mature Tamil war cycle.
Tamil tradition presents Siṃhamukha as another brother of Tāraka.

Siṃhamukha.myth: The asura brothers wage war against Murukaṉ
Siṃhamukha.note: Tāraka and Siṃhamukha belong to the same allied asura campaign.

Siṃhikā.note: After Siṃhikā seizes his shadow, Hanuman enters her body and kills her.
Siṃhikā is securely listed as his sister in several Purāṇic genealogies.
Some variable Purāṇic genealogies make Siṃhikā his sister or half-sister.
Later two-halves tradition transfers Rāhu’s maternity to Ketu.
Siṃhikā is Rāhu’s mother in the dominant epic and Purāṇic genealogy.

Somaka.note: Nagalapuram tradition substitutes Somaka for Hayagrīva as the demon Matsya kills.

Spənta Mainyu.myth: Vayu moves between the rival creations
Spənta Mainyu.note: Iranian Vayu operates in the intermediate space between the good and evil creations.

Subhadrā.note: Subhadrā is Balarama’s sister in epic and Purāṇic genealogy.
Balabhadra, Subhadrā, and Jagannātha are jointly worshipped at Puri.
Some regional traditions identify the escaped goddess with Subhadrā.
His sister and the central member of Puri's temple triad.
She travels with Jagannath in her own chariot, Darpadalana or Devadalana.
Subhadrā is Krishna’s chief epic-Purāṇic sister.

Sudarśana.note: Hiraṇyākṣa hurls a trident, which the personified divine discus cuts apart.
The weapon-person shares Jagannath's altar as the fourth image.
Their wooden bodies are replaced together during Nabakalebara.
The personified divine discus functions as Krishna’s weapon and agent.
The divine discus severs Rāhu’s head after his theft of nectar.
Sudarśana forces Rāhu to retreat when he approaches Sun and Moon.

Sugriva.note: Lakshmana joins Rama’s alliance with Sugriva against their respective enemies.
Lakshmana angrily threatens Sugriva for delaying the promised search for Sita.

Sugrīva.note: Hanuman serves as Sugrīva’s minister and supports his alliance and kingship.
Rāma restores Sugrīva’s throne; Sugrīva supplies search and war forces.
Śumbha sends Sugrīva to demand that the Goddess choose either brother.
Sugrīva is generated through Sūrya’s divine agency in the vāṇara genealogy.
As Rāma, Vishnu allies with Sugrīva during the campaign against Rāvaṇa.

Suhotra.note: Suhotra is one of Paraśurāma’s elder brothers in the Vana Parvan.
Paraśurāma requests that Suhotra recover from Jamadagni’s curse or stupefaction.

Sumantra.note: Sumantra is named as one of Kalki’s brothers.

Sumati.note: The late biography names Sumati as Kalki’s mother.

Sumedhas.note: Śrīvidyā teaching attributed to Paraśurāma is transmitted through Sumedhas.

Sumālī.note: Ravana is the maternal grandson of the rākṣasa Sumālī.

Sunanda.note: Sunanda joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.
Sunanda fights or restrains Bali’s Asura forces as Vāmana’s attendant.

Sunda.note: Tilottamā provokes Sunda’s jealous claim, leading him to fight and die against Upasunda.
Śumbha is generated from Sunda following Sunda’s fatal encounter with Tilottamā.
Viśvakarman creates Tilottamā, whose beauty causes Sunda's fatal rivalry with Upasunda.

Sundareśvara.note: Through identification with Mīnākṣī, Pārvatī marries Śiva’s local Madurai form.

Sunīthā.note: Individual later genealogies assign Sunīthā as a daughter of Yama.

Suparṇī.note: Some later or regional traditions name Suparṇī as Garuḍa's wife.

Supārśva.note: The Rāmāyaṇa names Supārśva as Sampāti’s son.
Supārśva provides food for his aged, wingless father.
Supārśva reports seeing Rāvaṇa carrying Sītā southward through the sky.

Surabhi.note: Variable later genealogies list Surabhi as Aditi's sister and co-wife.
Surabhi supplies milk while Airāvata transports heavenly water for Kṛṣṇa’s consecration.
Surabhi is named among Daksha’s daughters and becomes an ancestral mother.
Surabhi and Indra jointly consecrate and honor Kṛṣṇa as Govinda.
A bovinizing Purāṇic genealogy names Nandin as Surabhi’s son.
Some epic-Purāṇic systems make the eleven Rudras offspring of Surabhi.
Surabhi is mother of the Rudras with Kaśyapa in several accounts.
Surabhi is mother of the Rudras with Brahmā in a variant genealogy.
Certain Purāṇic classifications place his equine lineage through Gāndharvī and Surabhi.

Surasā.note: Hanuman outwits Surasā’s demand to enter her mouth by changing size.

Surūpā.note: Later genealogical traditions variously name Surūpā as Bṛhaspati’s mother.

Sushena.note: Sushena diagnoses Lakshmana and prescribes medicinal herbs for his restoration.

Suvarcalā.note: Some regional Indian traditions give Suvarcalā as Hanuman’s wife.
Suvarcalā appears as an additional or alternative wife in particular later lists.

Suyaśā.note: Suyaśā, daughter of the Maruts, becomes Nandin’s wife.

Suṣeṇa.note: Rāmāyaṇa genealogical material associates the vāṇara Suṣeṇa with Varuṇa’s paternity or creative agency.

Svadhā.note: Svadhā is Daksha’s daughter and is given to the Pitṛs.

Svarbhānu.myth: Later assimilation of two eclipse beings
Svarbhānu.note: Later texts identify the Ṛgvedic eclipse asura Svarbhānu with Rāhu.
Svarbhānu pierces or conceals Sūrya with darkness.

Svāhā.note: Epic and Purāṇic tradition makes personified Svāhā the wife of Agni.
Svāhā desires Agni and approaches him disguised as sages’ wives.
Svāhā assumes other women’s forms to receive Agni’s seed.
Svāhā is Daksha’s daughter and is given to Agni.
Svāhā collects Agni’s seed and deposits it, thereby producing Skanda.
Svāhā claims Skanda as hers while the Mothers acquire him through adoption.
Mahābhārata variants include Svāhā among the figures involved in Skanda’s birth.
Svāhā impersonates six sages’ wives but cannot assume Arundhatī’s form.

Svāyambhuva Manu.note: Svāyambhuva Manu is listed among Brahmā's offspring or emanations.
Through Prasūti, Satī is a descendant of Svāyambhuva Manu.

Swami Samarth.note: Devotees identify Swami Samarth as Dattātreya or Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī's continuation.

Sādhyas.note: The Sādhyas occupy a succeeding solar-nectar level after the Ādityas.

Sādhyas.myth: Assembly of the gods in heaven
Sādhyas.note: The Sādhyas accompany the Vasus in the epic heavenly assembly.

Sāgara.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Sāgara.note: Sāgara and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Sāmba.note: Balarama coerces the Kurus into releasing the captured Sāmba.
Sāmba is an important son of Krishna.
Sāmba’s disguise deceives Nārada and the other sages during the fatal prank.
Nārada joins the sages whose curse produces the pestle destroying the Yādavas.
Sūrya cures Sāmba’s disfiguring skin disease after prolonged solar worship.

Sārasvata.note: Some variants make the sage Sārasvata the child of Sarasvatī and Dadhīci.
Sarasvatī sustains Sārasvata during famine, sometimes by supplying fish.

Sāriputta.note: The Ghata-jātaka identifies the Buddha’s disciple Sāriputta with Kaṇha in a former birth.

Sātvata.note: Sātvata joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.

Sātyaki.note: Sātyaki is presented as a heroic incarnation connected with a portion of the Maruts.

Sāvarṇi Manu.note: Sāvarṇi Manu, a child of Chāyā, is their half-brother.
Some genealogical arrangements make Sāvarṇi the half-brother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Shani and Sāvarṇi Manu are jointly named as children of Chāyā.
Sāvarṇi Manu, the future Manu, is born to Sūrya and Chāyā.
Sāvarṇi Manu, child of Chāyā and the Sun, is Yamī’s half-brother.
Later solar genealogy makes Sāvarṇi Manu Yamuna's half-brother through Chāyā.

Sūrapadman.note: Murukaṉ defeats Sūrapadman after a prolonged war against his forces.
Murukaṉ transforms the demon’s halves into his peacock mount and cock banner.

Takṣaka.note: Agni targets Takṣaka’s forest, though the nāga is absent during most burning.
Takṣaka is one of Śeṣa’s named nāga brothers.

Takṣaka.myth: Nāgas receive Balarāma’s returning serpent essence
Takṣaka.note: Takṣaka receives the thousand-headed serpent emerging from Balarāma at death.
Takṣaka is listed among Vāsuki’s brothers or close serpent kin.

Takṣaka.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Takṣaka.note: Takṣaka and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Taleju.note: Bhairava and Taleju occur within the same royal and civic ritual synthesis.

Tapatī.note: Tapatī, a daughter associated with Chāyā, is their half-sister.
Shani and Tapatī are jointly named as children of Chāyā and Sūrya.
Tapatī is a solar daughter who later marries King Saṃvaraṇa.
Tapatī, child of Chāyā and the Sun, is Yamī-Yamunā’s half-sister.
Later solar genealogy makes Tapatī Yamuna's half-sister through Chāyā.

Tejaprabhā Buddha.note: In East Asian Buddhist adaptation, the Nine Luminaries became attendants of Tejaprabhā Buddha.

The Bhṛgus.note: The Bhṛgus restore Bali after Indra kills him.
The Bhṛgus consecrate Bali, conduct his sacrifices, and strengthen his sovereignty.

The Eagle/Falcon.note: The celestial bird steals or retrieves Soma and carries him to the ritual community.

The Kṛttikās.note: Ganga shares or competes with the Kṛttikās in claiming Skanda’s maternity.

The Seven Sages.note: Skanda’s birth causes the sages’ wives to be falsely accused of infidelity.

The other twenty-six Nakshatras.note: Daksha’s other lunar-station daughters are Chandra’s neglected wives.
The neglected wives complain to Daksha that Chandra favors Rohiṇī.

Tilottamā.note: Tilottamā is the brothers’ indirect mother through the fatal encounter she induces.
Viśvakarman constructs her from minute portions of everything beautiful.

Timbarū.note: Pañcasikha loves Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, daughter of the Gandhabba king Timbarū.

Tirumūlar.note: Nandi serves as Tirumūlar’s divine guru in Tamil Śaiva lineage memory.

Trailokyavijaya.note: Trailokyavijaya subdues or tramples Rudra-Maheśvara in Buddhist tantric narratives.

Trayī.note: The personified Vedic category Trayī is made Savitr’s daughter.

Trijaṭā.note: Trijaṭā consoles Sītā and foretells Rāma’s victory.

Tripura asuras.note: Brahmā grants the asuras three cities or limited invulnerability.

Tripura's three demons.note: Śiva destroys the three demons and their aligned cities with one arrow.

Tripurasundarī.note: Tripurasundarī assumes Kāma’s sugarcane bow, five arrows, and creative power.
Some early Śrīvidyā structures retain Kāmadeva in a subordinate consort role.

Tripurasundarī.myth: Tripurasundarī emanates Bagalāmukhī from turmeric lake
Tripurasundarī.note: Tripurasundarī emits Bagalāmukhī in response to Viṣṇu’s austerities.
Paraśurāma becomes a devotee and promulgator of Tripurasundarī’s ritual method.

Tripura’s asuras.note: Śiva destroys the asuras’ three aligned cities with one cosmic shot.

Tripurā.note: Dattātreya reveals Tripurā as supreme consciousness in his instruction to Paraśurāma.

Tripurāsuras.myth: Śiva’s campaign against the triple cities
Tripurāsuras.note: Nandin serves in Śiva’s campaign against the demons of Tripura.

Trita Āptya.note: Trita kills Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son and releases cattle, under Indra’s impetus.

Triśiras.note: Triśiras appears as Ravana’s son in differing genealogical lists.

Tumburu.note: Nārada and Tumburu appear together as exemplary celestial musicians.
Later narratives sometimes make Nārada and Tumburu rivals in musical excellence.

Tuṅgavidyā.myth: Tuṅgavidyā coordinates music and the lovers’ meetings
Tuṅgavidyā.note: She assists Radha through music, messages, reconciliation, and rendezvous.

Tvaṣṭṛ.note: Obscure Ṛgvedic formulations connect Agni’s birth with Tvaṣṭṛ’s activity or daughters.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashions the vajra that Indra uses against Vṛtra.
Vedic birth poetry presents Tvaṣṭṛ in an unstable paternal or adversarial relationship with Indra.
After Indra kills Viśvarūpa, Tvaṣṭṛ performs a rite producing Vṛtra against him.
Pūṣan’s goat precedes the horse so Tvaṣṭṛ may prepare the offering.
An early genealogy makes Tvaṣṭṛ Saraṇyū’s father; later variants assign his role to Viśvakarman.
Later texts merge or alternate the two divine craftsman figures.
Community genealogies name Tvaṣṭṛ among Viśvakarman's five artisan sons.
Tvaṣṭṛ produces Vṛtra from sacrificial residue or fire after Viśvarūpa's killing.
Tvaṣṭṛ creates Vṛtra to avenge Indra's killing of his son Viśvarūpa.

Tvaṣṭṛ.myth: Twins fashioned together in the womb
Tvaṣṭṛ.note: Yamī argues that Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned her and Yama together as a pair.

Tāmra.note: Variable later genealogies list Tāmra as Aditi's sister and co-wife.

Tāraka.note: Brahmā grants that only a son of Śiva can kill Tāraka.

Tārakākṣa.note: Tārakākṣa is one of Tāraka’s three sons and Tripura rulers.

Tārā.note: Tārā is Bṛhaspati’s wife in the mature epic-Purāṇic genealogy.
Bṛhaspati’s side secures Tārā’s return after Soma refuses demands for restitution.
Tārā bears Budha after her union with Soma.
Budha reproaches or threatens his silent mother until she names Soma.
Some versions say Soma seduces Tārā; others describe abduction or mutual elopement.
Soma and Tārā are Budha’s parents after disputed paternity.
Some eastern Tantric systems strongly assimilate Kālī and Tārā while others preserve their distinction.
Tārā diplomatically calms Lakshmana’s anger during his confrontation with Sugriva.

Tāṭakā.note: At Viśvāmitra’s direction, Rāma kills Tāṭakā.

Tīrthaṅkaras.note: Jain Gandharvas attend ordered celestial assemblies honoring the Tīrthaṅkaras.

Tṛṇāvarta.note: The whirlwind demon attacks Kṛṣṇa as an agent commonly commissioned by Kamsa.
The infant Krishna kills the whirlwind-demon that carries him away.
As the child Kṛṣṇa, Vishnu defeats the whirlwind demon Tṛṇāvarta.

Ugajin.note: Benzaiten fuses with the serpentine food, fertility, water, and prosperity deity Ugajin.

Ugracaṇḍā.myth: Recurrent buffalo conflict in another cosmic cycle
Ugracaṇḍā.note: Ugracaṇḍā kills a form of Mahiṣa in one recurring cosmic cycle.

Ulmuka.note: Ulmuka is commonly listed as a child of Balarama and Revatī.

Umā.note: Later tradition identifies Umā as Rudra-Śiva's consort and divine power.
Umā gives alms to Vāmana in his initiated Brahmin-student form.

Umā Haimavatī.note: Umā reveals that the Yakṣa was Brahman and the victory belonged to it.
Umā reveals to Indra that the vanished yaksha was Brahman.

Unnati.note: Some later or regional traditions name Unnati as Garuḍa's wife.

Upananda.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Upananda.note: Upananda and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Upasunda.note: Tilottamā provokes Upasunda’s jealous claim, leading him to fight and die against Sunda.
Viśvakarman creates Tilottamā, whose beauty causes Upasunda's fatal rivalry with Sunda.

Urvaśī.note: Her presence or sight occasions the seminal event producing Vasiṣṭha and later Agastya.
Seeing Urvaśī causes Varuṇa and Mitra to emit the seed used in the vessel birth.

Urvāśī.note: Gandharvas perform in her celestial court narratives and stories involving Purūravas.
At Indra’s court Urvāśī propositions Arjuna; Indra later limits her curse.

Utathya.note: Utathya is Bṛhaspati’s elder brother and Mamatā’s husband.

Utpalaka.myth: Eight Great Nāga Kings attend Buddha
Utpalaka.note: Utpalaka and Vāsuki jointly attend the Buddha with immense retinues.

Utsarga.note: Late genealogical catalogues list Utsarga among Mitra's children.

Uttānapāda.note: Uttānapāda is commonly listed as a child of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.

Uṣas.note: Uṣas is poetically called the visible face of Aditi.
Agni is kindled as Uṣas appears and carries the daybreak worship.
Uṣas awakens or precedes worship as the twins arrive with the dawn.
The Dawns are asked to approach the rite and convey or reveal Bhaga.
Uṣas is repeatedly called the daughter of Heaven.

Uṣas.myth: Father places seed in daughter's womb
Uṣas.note: A disputed interpretation identifies Heaven as the father impregnating Uṣas.
Indra shatters Uṣas’s wagon and causes her to flee.
Some early versions identify Prajāpati's daughter as Uṣas or Dawn.

Uṣas.myth: Father and daughter assume deer forms
Uṣas.note: Prajāpati desires, pursues, or unites with Dawn, sometimes while both take deer forms.
Uṣas is explicitly named as Rātrī’s sister and temporal counterpart.
Rātrī establishes or displaces Dawn, who subsequently clears the darkness.
Mother Night entrusts protected worshippers to Dawn for the next temporal passage.
She is the daughter or female form whose violation Rudra avenges.
Uṣas reveals, precedes, or poetically gives birth to Sūrya.
Fluid Vedic poetry sometimes describes Dawn as Sūrya’s wife or companion.
Uṣas appears within the ordered cosmos guarded by Varuṇa, without substantial direct interaction.
Vṛtra's defeat is associated with Indra's production or revelation of Uṣas.

Vaivasvata Manu.note: Vaivasvata Manu is Shani’s half-brother, born to Sūrya and Saṃjñā.
Solar genealogies list Manu as Yamī-Yamunā’s brother.

Vaiśravaṇa.note: Sarasvatī and Vaiśravaṇa jointly protect the scripture and the state.

Vaiṣṇavī.note: Vaiṣṇavī participates among the Mothers opposing Andhaka’s blood-born forms.
Kālī and Vaiṣṇavī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.
She struck him with her discus, producing thousands of blood-born counterparts.
Vaiṣṇavī fights the brothers’ army with discus and Garuḍa-associated form.

Vajrapāṇi.note: Hayagrīva and Vajrapāṇi appear jointly in tantric assemblies and protector systems.
Vajrapāṇi subdues, tramples, kills, converts, or incorporates Rudra into a maṇḍala.
Vajrapāṇi appears as a yaksha-like or explicitly yaksha protector before developing into a great bodhisattva.

Vajravārāhī.note: Hayagrīva and Vajravārāhī are paired in prominent Nyingma tantric cycles.

Vajrāṅga.note: Developed Purāṇic genealogy names Vajrāṅga as Tāraka’s father.

Vala.note: Bṛhaspati splits Vala’s rock enclosure and takes the imprisoned cattle.
Vala laments the cattle Bṛhaspati removed after breaking the enclosure.
Indra breaks Vala’s cave or fortress and releases cattle and light.

Valli.note: Valli, the hunter-princess, becomes Murukaṉ’s regional Tamil consort.

Valli.myth: Murukaṉ courts Valli in several disguises
Valli.note: Murukaṉ repeatedly propositions Valli as hunter, ascetic, or other disguised figure.

Valli.myth: Disguised Murukaṉ stages an elephant rescue
Valli.note: Murukaṉ conceals his identity and uses Gaṇeśa’s elephant disguise to secure Valli’s promise.

Varuṇa's sons.note: Rāvaṇa campaigns against Varuṇa's sons and other aquatic divine powers.

Varuṇānī.note: Later sources commonly make Varuṇānī his consort, though Varuṇī may remain an independent liquor goddess.

Varuṇī.note: Varuṇī emerges from a tree and intoxicates Balarama and his companions.
The goddess of liquor emerges during the churning supported by Kūrma.
Varuṇī intoxicates Balarāma immediately before his coercive command to Yamuna.

Varāhī.note: Varāha produces or corresponds to Varāhī, who joins the Mātṛkās in battle.

Varāṅgī.note: Developed Purāṇic genealogy names Varāṅgī as Tāraka’s mother.

Varṇinī.myth: Chinnamastā feeds attendants with her blood
Varṇinī.note: One lateral blood stream from Chinnamastā’s neck feeds Varṇinī.

Vasanta.note: Vasanta creates the sensuous flowering environment for Kāma’s attack on Śiva.
Divine Spring accompanies Kāma and consoles Rati after his burning.

Vasiṣṭha.note: Urvaśī is linked to Vasiṣṭha’s extraordinary conception through Mitra and Varuṇa’s emitted seed.
Vasiṣṭha is frequently listed among Brahmā's mind-born or bodily sons.
As Vasu Dyu, he steals Vasiṣṭha's wish-granting cow with the Vasus.
Vasiṣṭha curses Dyu to a long, childless human life for the theft.

Vasiṣṭha.myth: Vasiṣṭha’s cow sustains sacrifice and hospitality
Vasiṣṭha.note: Nandinī or Śabalā supplies Vasiṣṭha’s rites and inexhaustible hospitality.
With Vasiṣṭha’s authorization, Śabalā generates armies against the king’s forces.

Vasiṣṭha.myth: Vasiṣṭha seeks Tārā rites at Mahācīna
Vasiṣṭha.note: Vasiṣṭha curses Tārā, then travels to learn her left-hand worship.
Mitra and Varuṇa are jointly involved in Vasiṣṭha's extraordinary origin involving Urvaśī.
Vasiṣṭha is jointly classified among the mind-born Prajāpatis.
Vasiṣṭha instructs the young Rāma in nondual philosophy.

Vasiṣṭha.myth: Vasiṣṭha and the river of blood
Vasiṣṭha.note: Sarasvatī carries Vasiṣṭha toward his enemy but sweeps him away to safety.
Vasiṣṭha arises from seed emitted by Mitra and Varuṇa after they behold Urvaśī.
Vasiṣṭha curses the Vasus to human birth, then shortens seven sentences.

Vasu.note: Vasu is one of Paraśurāma’s elder brothers in the Vana Parvan.
Paraśurāma requests that Vasu recover from Jamadagni’s curse or stupefaction.
Dakṣa's daughter Vasu bears the eight Vasus to Dharma.

Vasudeva.note: Vasudeva is Balarama’s father in epic and Purāṇic genealogy.
As Kṛṣṇa, Jagannath is the son of Vasudeva.
Krishna is the biological son of Vasudeva and Devakī.
Vithoba inherits Kṛṣṇa’s father through identification with Kṛṣṇa.
Yamuna lowers or yields so Vasudeva can carry infant Krishna safely to Gokula.

Vasudhārā.note: Jambhala is paired with Vasudhārā as an abundance couple in Himalayan Buddhism.

Vasumat.note: Some Purāṇic lists substitute Vasumat among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons.

Vasundharā.note: Nepalese tradition equates them through grain, wealth, and abundance.

Vavar.note: Ayyappa and Vavar initially fight and become mutually impressed.
Vavar becomes Ayyappa's ally and assists his campaign against Mahiṣi.
Government pilgrimage tradition describes Vavar as Ayyappa's trusted lieutenant.

Vedavatī.note: After Rāvaṇa assaults her, Vedavatī curses him and is linked to Sītā's rebirth.
Ravana attempts to violate Vedavatī, who enters fire rather than submit.
Vedavatī curses Ravana and vows to return as the cause of his destruction.
Later tradition presents Sītā as Vedavatī reborn to destroy Rāvaṇa.

Venkateśvara.note: Tirumala traditions link Śrī-Lakṣmī to Venkateśvara through marriage and separation.

Vepacitti.note: Sakka battles and captures the asura ruler Vepacitti.
Sakka debates Vepacitti in narratives advocating patience and restrained sovereignty.

Vessavaṇa.note: Vessavaṇa governs a lower heaven and attends Sakka within Buddhist cosmology.

Vetāla.note: The blood-receiving Vetāla may locally be interpreted as Bhairava himself.

Veṅkaṭeśvara.note: Varāha grants Śrīnivāsa land in exchange for first worship and first food offering.

Vibhīṣaṇa.note: Brahmā grants Vibhīṣaṇa righteousness or immortality-like protection.
Tamil shrine legends connect Gaṇeśa, Vibhīṣaṇa, and the Śrīraṅgam image.
Vibhīṣaṇa prevents Hanuman’s execution by invoking the legal immunity of envoys.
Vibhīṣaṇa later fights beside Hanuman and Rāma’s allied forces.
Vibhīṣaṇa is Kubera’s paternal half-brother in the dominant genealogy.
Vibhīṣaṇa identifies Kubera’s former Puṣpaka and offers it to Rāma.
Lakshmana supports Rama’s alliance with Ravana’s defecting brother Vibhīṣaṇa.
Vibhīṣaṇa reveals Indrajit’s ritual vulnerability and guides Lakshmana into battle.
Rāma grants refuge to Rāvaṇa’s defecting brother despite allied suspicion.
Rāma grants Vibhīṣaṇa the kingship of Laṅkā.

Vibhīṣaṇa.myth: Vibhīṣaṇa defects before the Laṅkā war
Vibhīṣaṇa.note: Ravana rejects Vibhīṣaṇa’s counsel, causing him to join Rāma.

Vidyunmālin.note: Nandin kills or, in variant wording, defeats the demon Vidyunmālin.
Vidyunmālin is one of Tāraka’s three sons and Tripura rulers.

Vijaya.note: Vijaya joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.
As Jaya, he shares exile and three paired hostile births with Vijaya.
The standard later pairing identifies Hiraṇyākṣa individually with Vijaya.
Vijaya is named as a son of Kalki and Padmāvatī.
Narasimha’s killing advances the cursed gatekeepers’ eventual restoration to Viṣṇu.
Vijaya informs Satī of the sacrifice and insult in one variant.
Vijaya fights or restrains Bali’s Asura forces as Vāmana’s attendant.
Vijaya serves as one of Vishnu’s gatekeepers.
Vishnu repeatedly kills Vijaya during the gatekeeper’s cursed births as divine enemies.

Vijaykumar Naidu.note: Oneness devotees treated Vijaykumar Naidu as Kalki or a vehicle of universal divine consciousness.

Vikoka.note: Kalki kills Vikoka simultaneously with Koka because each revives while the other lives.

Vimalā.note: Jagannath's food becomes mahāprasāda after its ritual presentation to Vimalā.

Vinatā.note: Variable later genealogies list Vinatā as Aditi's sister and co-wife.
Vinatā is named among Daksha’s daughters and becomes an ancestral mother.
Garuḍa obtains amṛta as ransom to free his enslaved mother.
Purāṇic genealogy makes Vinatā Jatāyu’s ancestor through her son Aruṇa.
Kadru's deception makes Vinatā a slave to Kadru and the Nāgas.
Sampāti belongs to the avian lineage descended from Vinatā.
Vinatā is Śeṣa’s half-aunt or stepmother through Kaśyapa.
Vinatā correctly calls him white but loses the rigged wager and becomes enslaved.

Vindhya.note: Vindhya receives the newborn boys and has his wife raise them.

Vindhyavāsinī.note: Later traditions identify the escaped Yogamāyā with the Vindhyan goddess Vindhyavāsinī.
Vindhyavāsinī’s martial description was adapted into the weapon-bearing Buddhist Sarasvatī tradition.

Vināyakī.note: An independent Mātṛkā or Yoginī was later variably assimilated as female Gaṇeśa.

Vipracitti.note: Vipracitti serves as a commander whom Bali orders to stop fighting.
One transferred genealogy makes Ketu the son of Siṃhikā and Vipracitti.
Vipracitti is usually named as Rāhu’s father in Purāṇic genealogy.

Virajā.myth: Radha’s jealous approach sends Virajā into river form
Virajā.note: Virajā becomes a river when Radha approaches Krishna’s secluded meeting.

Virocana.note: Bali is consistently identified as Virocana’s son.
Bali reflects upon Virocana’s teaching while pursuing self-knowledge in Pātāla.
Virocana is Hiranyakashipu’s grandson through Prahlāda.
Indra rejects the bodily-self doctrine that fellow student Virocana accepts.
Prajāpati teaches Virocana, who departs mistakenly believing the adorned body is the self.

Virūpakkha.note: Vessavaṇa acts jointly with Virūpakkha as one of the Four Great Kings.

Virūpākṣa.note: Through identification with Pampa, Pārvatī becomes consort of Śiva’s local form.

Virūḷhaka.note: Vessavaṇa acts jointly with Virūḷhaka as one of the Four Great Kings.

Vivasvat.note: Later tradition identifies the rejected Mārtāṇḍa with Vivasvat.
Vivasvat becomes a named Āditya in later Vedic and epic genealogies.
Tvaṣṭṛ arranges for Vivasvat to receive his daughter Saraṇyū as wife.

Viśravas.note: The dominant epic-Purāṇic genealogy makes Viśravas Kubera’s father.
Viśravas fathers Ravana by the rākṣasī Kaikasī.
Some Purāṇic genealogical variants derive the yakshas through Viśravas.

Viśvaksena.note: Viśvaksena joins Viṣṇu’s attendants in repelling Bali’s attacking followers.
Bhairava kills or impales Viṣṇu’s guardian after being barred.
Viśvaksena.source: Purāṇic and South Indian iconographic sources

Viśvaksena.note: Viśvaksena fights or restrains Bali’s Asura forces as Vāmana’s attendant.

Viśvamohinī.note: Nārada seeks Viśvamohinī but is humiliated and loses at her marriage contest.

Viśvarūpa.note: Viśvarūpa replaces Bṛhaspati as the devas’ priest after Bṛhaspati withdraws.
Indra kills Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son for divided loyalty or threatening power.
Tvaṣṭṛ is father of the three-headed Viśvarūpa, whose killing begins the revenge cycle.
Late merged genealogies make Viśvakarman Viśvarūpa's father instead of Tvaṣṭṛ.

Viśvāmitra.note: Under Indra’s command, Menakā distracts Viśvāmitra and lives with him for years.
Menakā and Viśvāmitra form a long sexual union that produces Śakuntalā.
Viśvāmitra detects Rambhā’s mission and curses her into stone for ten thousand years.
Śabalā creates armies that destroy Viśvāmitra’s army and sons.
Viśvāmitra receives Lakshmana and Rama as pupils and sacrificial defenders.
Viśvāmitra teaches Rāma divine weapons and guides his early exploits.

Viśvāmitra.myth: Vasiṣṭha and the river of blood
Viśvāmitra.note: Ordered to deliver Vasiṣṭha, Sarasvatī instead saves him through her river course.

Viśvāmitra.myth: Vasiṣṭha and the river of blood
Viśvāmitra.note: Viśvāmitra curses Sarasvatī to flow with blood after she saves Vasiṣṭha.

Viśvāvasu.note: Menakā unites with the gandharva Viśvāvasu and bears Pramadvarā.
Viśvāvasu is one of Paraśurāma’s elder brothers in the Vana Parvan.
Paraśurāma requests that Viśvāvasu recover from Jamadagni’s curse or stupefaction.

Viśākha.note: Viśākha emerges from Skanda’s wound or divided body as a second youth.

Viśākha.myth: Skanda and Viśākha appear as distinct figures
Viśākha.note: Epic narrative and Kushan coins can present Viśākha beside Skanda.
Later tradition absorbs the once-distinguishable Viśākha as a name of Skanda.

Viśākhā.myth: Viśākhā carries messages between the divine lovers
Viśākhā.note: Viśākhā serves Radha as a principal companion and messenger.

Viśālākṣī.note: Later Kāśī worship and Carnatic music merge her with the wide-eyed goddess.
The Vārāṇasī goddess is incorporated into regional Pārvatī and Śakti theology.

Viṣṇudūtas.note: Viṣṇudūtas debate and repel Yama’s messengers, preventing Ajāmila’s seizure.

Viṣṇuyaśas.note: Later Purāṇic tradition makes Kalki the son of Śambhala’s chief Brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas.

Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras.note: Variable lists align the ten Mahāvidyās pairwise with Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras.

Viṣṭi.note: Some variant genealogies include Viṣṭi among Chāyā’s children with Shani.

Vyomāsura.note: Krishna kills the sky-demon after he abducts cowherd boys.

Vyāghrapāda.myth: Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda witness Śiva’s dance
Vyāghrapāda.note: Vyāghrapāda joins Śeṣa’s Patañjali incarnation in worship and witnessing the dance.

Vyāhṛti.note: The personified ritual category Vyāhṛti is made Savitr’s daughter.

Vyāsa.note: Appearing as a housewife, she feeds the alms-denied Vyāsa and averts his curse.
The Bengali poem elaborates her feeding or releasing the afflicted sage.
Gaṇeśa writes while Vyāsa dictates under mutually imposed conditions.
Later tellings say Gaṇeśa breaks his tusk to continue Vyāsa’s dictation.

Vyāsa.myth: Madhva meets Vyāsa and receives instruction
Vyāsa.note: Vāyu’s third incarnation Madhva receives authoritative instruction from Vyāsa.

Vāc.note: Prajāpati joins or creates with personified Speech, producing beings and ritual order.
Some variants identify personified Speech as the female being generated by Brahmā.
Brahmā sexually desires Vāc in variants reworking the Vedic daughter motif.
The gods exchange Vāc for Soma; she later chooses and returns to them.
The gods exchange Vāc for Soma; attracted by their singing, she later returns.
The Cow named Vāc and Virāj is called Kāma’s daughter.
Vāc declares that she sustains the paired Mitra–Varuṇa within her cosmic activity.
Vāc accompanies or mates with Prajāpati in generating beings and ritual forms.
Brāhmaṇa theology explicitly declares that Speech is Sarasvatī.

Vāc.myth: Production of eight Vasus from Speech
Vāc.note: An altar-theology account says Vāc produced the eight Vasus.

Vāc.myth: Speech challenges the supremacy of breath
Vāc.note: Speech can depart without killing the body but fails when chief breath prepares to leave.
Viśvakarman is identified with speech and produces creatures through it.

Vāgdevīs.note: Hayagrīva transmits the thousand names composed by the Vāgdevīs.

Vālin.note: Rāma shoots Vālin from concealment and defends it as royal punishment.

Vānaras.note: Apsarases and other supernatural females bear some vānaras fathered by divine males.

Vāruṇī.note: Vāruṇī accompanies Śeṣa in the Purāṇic description of his subterranean realm.
Vāruṇī provides divine liquor for Śeṣa’s incarnation Balarāma.

Vārāhī.note: Vārāhī consumes Andhaka’s blood or fights the duplicates it produces.
Kālī and Vārāhī fight together within the Goddess’s power-host.
She struck him with a sword.
The later account emphasizes her tusks in the attack upon him.
Vārāhī fights the brothers’ army in boar-associated form.

Vāstu-puruṣa.note: The guardians join numerous gods in overpowering and occupying the cosmic being’s body.
Vāstu-puruṣa.source: Matsya Purāṇa; Bṛhat Saṃhitā; architectural manuals

Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī.note: Later Datta communities include Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī among Dattātreya's manifestations.

Vāta.note: Early hymns distinguish Vāta from Vāyu, but later lexicons and mythography merge them.

Vīrabhadra.note: Vīrabhadra fights Andhaka or his army in later Śaiva retellings.
Vīrabhadra throws Bhaga down and tears out his eyes.
Vīrabhadra attacks Daksha and destroys his sacrificial assembly.
Vīrabhadra beheads Daksha and casts his head into the fire.
A Matsya Purāṇa tradition equates Aṅgāraka with Śiva’s fierce agent Vīrabhadra.
Gupta and medieval panels repeatedly place Vīrabhadra as a framing guardian beside the Mothers.
Nandin joins Vīrabhadra and Śiva’s hosts in destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Some Śaiva recensions send Vīrabhadra to overcome the uncontrollably raging Narasimha.
Śiva’s dispatched warrior Vīrabhadra knocks out Pūṣan’s teeth.
A Skanda Purāṇa variant says Vīrabhadra breaks Pūṣan’s teeth because he laughed.
Śiva emanates Vīrabhadra from his wrath to destroy Dakṣa's rite.
Vīrabhadra executes Śiva's vengeance against Dakṣa and the assembled gods.
Created after Satī’s death, Vīrabhadra avenges her by destroying the rite.
Śiva creates or commissions Vīrabhadra to devastate Dakṣa’s rite.
Dhere proposes affinity or transformation between Vithoba and regional Vīrabhadra traditions.
Vīrabhadra.source: Dhere, Rise of a Folk God

Vīraka.note: The gaṇa Vīraka blocks Andhaka’s attempt to seize Pārvatī.

Vīriṇī.note: Epic tradition names Vīriṇī as Daksha’s wife.
Some genealogies name Vīriṇī or Asiknī as Satī’s mother.

Vṛṣabha.myth: Medieval fusion of attendant and vehicle
Vṛṣabha.note: Later iconography and practice increasingly identify Nandin with Śiva’s bull.

Vṛṣaparvan.note: Śukra serves Vṛṣaparvan and threatens departure unless Devayānī’s demand is met.

Weituo.myth: Buddhist Skanda becomes an armored monastery guardian
Weituo.note: East Asian Buddhism developed transmitted Skanda traditions into the guardian Weituo.

Wēšparkar.note: Wēšparkar is an eastern-Iranian development possibly connected with Vayu uparō.kairyō.

Yajña.note: Excluded Rudra pierces, wounds, or disrupts the personified sacrifice.

Yakṣī.note: Yakṣī is named as Kubera’s consort in some differing textual traditions.

Yalambar.myth: Severed king’s head installed as Ākāś Bhairab
Yalambar.note: Later Kathmandu legend identifies Ākāś Bhairab with the deified king Yalambar.

Yama.note: Yama descends from the Āditya Vivasvat.
Some later enumerations count Yama himself among the Ādityas.
Agni guides or transfers the deceased toward Yama’s ancestral realm.
Yama and the Aśvins are children of Vivasvant and Saraṇyū.

Yama.myth: Kālabhairava’s authority over death in Kāśī
Yama.note: Bhairava’s jurisdiction over death can supersede Yama’s authority within Kāśī.
Yama’s staff is broken during the assault in some accounts.
Yama gives the Goddess a staff.

Yama.myth: Watery parentage of Yama and Yamī
Yama.note: An obscure verse associates the watery Gandharva and a water-woman with Yama’s origin.
Yama grants Hanuman a protective boon in expanded childhood accounts.
Hiranyakashipu appropriates Yama’s cosmic office during his universal rule.
Yama protests that Jagannath's sacred field liberates souls and empties his jurisdiction.
In some versions Krishna retrieves his teacher’s dead son from Yama’s realm.
Yama and Kubera share world-guardian functions and appear in divine delegations.
Mahiṣa appropriates Yama's authority over death after conquering heaven.
Solar genealogies make Yama the brother or half-brother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Nandin accompanies Śiva during intervention against Yama in the Śveta-type cycle.
Nārada warns Yama that Rāvaṇa is approaching to challenge him.
Yama joins the directional gods who bless Narasimha’s Ahobilam wedding.

Yama.myth: Journey to the realm of the dead
Yama.note: Pūṣan guides the dead while Yama governs or receives them at their destination.
Rāvaṇa fights Yama until Brahmā intervenes to preserve his boon.
Yama’s private summons precipitates Lakṣmaṇa’s sacrifice and Rāma’s departure.

Yama.myth: Invasion of the realm of death
Yama.note: Ravana battles Yama until Brahmā intervenes to protect his boon.
Śiva defeats or restrains Yama to prevent Mārkaṇḍeya's death.
Savitr guides the departed along the righteous path associated with Yama.
Yama is Shani’s half-brother through their common father Sūrya.
Śiva strikes or restrains Yama while protecting Mārkaṇḍeya.
The brothers appropriate Yama’s cosmic authority.
Yama is the son of Vivasvant or Sūrya and Saraṇyū.
Sūrya investigates Chāyā after she curses Yama and exposes her identity.
Tvaṣṭṛ is Yama’s maternal grandfather through his daughter Saraṇyū.
Yama and Varuṇa are fellow directional guardians whose halls and weapons are juxtaposed.
Viśvakarman constructs Yama's celestial assembly hall.
Yāmī and Yama are primordial twins, later identified as Yamuna and Yama.
Yāmī proposes incestuous procreation, but Yama refuses on moral and cosmic grounds.
Yamuna welcomes and feeds Yama, who grants protection to brothers honoring sisters.

Yamadūtas.note: Yama’s messengers seize or escort the dead and execute his jurisdiction.

Yamāntaka.myth: Buddhist transfer of Bhairava’s name and iconography
Yamāntaka.note: Buddhists adapted Bhairava imagery for Yamāntaka without identifying the deities.
Mañjuśrī assumes the Yamāntaka form to overcome Yama or death.

Yaśas.note: Yaśas is paired with Harṣa as Rati’s child in one genealogy.

Yaśodā.note: As Kṛṣṇa, Jagannath is the foster son of Yaśodā.
Yaśodā raises Krishna as her foster-child and binds him to a mortar.

Yogamāyā.note: Yogamāyā transfers Balarama’s embryo from Devakī’s womb into Rohiṇī’s.
The goddess exchanges places with Krishna, escapes Kaṃsa, and reveals her divine form.
Pāñcarātra theology identifies Yogamāyā as a form of Mahālakṣmī.

Yogamāyā.myth: Yogamāyā arranges the lovers’ Vraja meetings
Yogamāyā.note: She orchestrates circumstances enabling Radha and Krishna’s intimate līlā.
Yogamāyā moves the embryo called Śeṣa from Devakī into Rohiṇī.
The goddess withdraws from sleeping Viṣṇu while Śeṣa supports the developed cosmic scene.
Yogamāyā transfers or substitutes children and carries out Vishnu-Kṛṣṇa’s birth plan.

Yoganidrā.note: Later Śākta theology interprets cosmic Night as Yoganidrā, the Goddess’s sleep-power within Viṣṇu.

Yoginīs.note: Bhairava acts as lord, guardian, or participant in Yoginī rites.

Yudhiṣṭhira.note: Kubera receives Yudhiṣṭhira after Bhīma’s violence and explains Maṇimat’s prior curse.
The lake yaksha tests Yudhiṣṭhira with ethical and theological questions and approves his answers.
Through the later Yama-Dharma equation, Yama is treated as Yudhiṣṭhira’s divine father.
Dharma tests Yudhiṣṭhira through riddles; identifying the tester as Yama is later harmonization.
Dharma tests Yudhiṣṭhira’s loyalty as a dog; later interpretation identifies Dharma with Yama.

Yājñavalkya.note: The deified sage Yājñavalkya serves as Kalki’s priest during the restoration.

Zadkiel.note: Western esoteric correspondence systems map Bṛhaspati to Jupiter’s archangel Zadkiel.

Zuhal.note: Arabic Zuhal corresponds astronomically to Shani but is not a Sanskrit epithet.

a monk.note: A Great Brahmā claims omniscience publicly, then privately admits ignorance to a monk.

al-Zuhara.note: Arabic-Persian and Indian astral systems assign these figures to Venus.

all the gods.note: A universalizing Vedic verse identifies Aditi with all the gods.

an unnamed Great Brahmā.note: Buddhist cosmology applies Brahmā's name to finite high gods rather than one eternal creator.

anti-gods.note: As Mohinī, Vishnu deceives the anti-gods and distributes amṛta to the gods.

devas reborn in a Brahmā realm.note: Later arrivals mistake the first-reborn Brahmā being for their creator.

five-headed dragon.note: Benzaiten morally transforms the destructive dragon, who promises to stop harming people.
After submitting and reforming, the dragon becomes Benzaiten’s spouse or guardian.

gaṇas.note: The gaṇas form Śiva's divine host of attendants.

ketakī flower.myth: False witness at the fiery column
ketakī flower.note: Brahmā recruits the falling ketakī as false witness that he reached the summit.

seven sisters.note: Her Vedic epithet “seven-sistered” associates her with a complex of divine rivers.

the Aṅgirases.note: Aryaman helps milk a cow that the gods gave to the Aṅgirases.
Bṛhaspati leads or acts with the priestly singers to recover cattle and light.

the Carṣaṇis.note: The Carṣaṇis are collectively named as the offspring of Aryaman and Mātṛkā.

the Daityas.note: Dattātreya engineers the Daityas' loss of merit and enables their defeat.

the Daśamahāvidyās.myth: Manifestation of the ten great forms
the Daśamahāvidyās.note: Satī manifests ten terrifying Goddess forms when Śiva obstructs her departure.

the Devas.note: Buddha weakens the gods’ enemies by stripping away their Vedic protection.
The Devas seek Dattātreya, follow his strategy, defeat the Daityas, and bow.

the Fathers.myth: Conveying the dead to the Fathers
the Fathers.note: Agni matures the corpse and conveys the deceased toward the Fathers.

the Fathers.myth: Guiding the dead to the Fathers
the Fathers.note: Pūṣan conducts the deceased safely along the road toward the Fathers.

the Four Great Kings.note: The Four Great Kings rule beneath Tāvatiṃsa and attend Sakka.
The Four Great Kings command yaksha armies and deploy them to protect the Buddhist community.

the Goddess’s lion.note: Niśumbha strikes the lion’s head before the Goddess destroys his weapons.

the Kṛttikās.myth: The Kṛttikās nurse Tāraka’s destined killer
the Kṛttikās.note: The Kṛttikās nurse or collectively mother Skanda, indirectly enabling Tāraka’s defeat.

the Mothers.note: He struck each Mother with his mace while their attacks multiplied him.

the Paṇis.note: Indra opposes the Paṇis and participates in recovering their hidden cattle.
Pūṣan’s awl pierces or softens the Paṇi’s heart to release hidden goods.

the Pitṛs.note: Aryaman is presented as the Pitṛs’ foremost representative or lord.
Yama rules or gathers with the ancestral fathers in their otherworldly community.

the Pracetas.note: Satī descends from the Pracetas in Dakṣa’s alternative rebirth genealogy.

the Pāṇḍavas.note: Citraratha gives the Pāṇḍavas supernatural horses after making peace with Arjuna.
After conflicts with yaksha guardians, Kubera receives the Pāṇḍavas favorably in his realm.

the Rivers.note: Vṛtra checks the Rivers' courses until Indra strikes him and opens their channels.

the Seven Seers.note: The Seven Seers give Vāmana kuśa grass.

the Tīrthaṅkaras.note: Indras perform ceremonial homage at Tīrthaṅkara births, renunciations, and enlightenments.
Medieval Jain systems assign each Tīrthaṅkara a subordinate yaksha and yakshi protecting the Jina’s teaching.

the Waters.note: Agni is paradoxically born or found within the divine Waters.
Vṛtra restrains the divine Waters until Indra breaks their enclosure.
After his defeat, the released Waters flow over and carry away Vṛtra's corpse.

the Yoginīs.note: Medieval systems make the Matrikas mothers, leaders, or prototypes of Yoginī clans.
Some system-dependent traditions equate or overlap Matrikas with Yoginīs.

the daughters of Dakṣa.note: Satī has numerous sisters whose names and numbers vary among genealogies.

the devas.note: The gods require Ayyappa to defeat Mahiṣi and praise him afterward.
Hayagrīva oppresses the devas, who seek a means to destroy him.

the divine mothers.note: The divine mothers authorize the consecration in which Airāvata supplies heavenly water.
Later interpretations make the divine mothers direct Surabhi’s consecration of Kṛṣṇa.

the dogs of Yama.myth: Guardians of the road to the dead
the dogs of Yama.note: Two four-eyed dogs watch, track, and guard the road leading to Yama.

the eight Mothers.myth: Directional pairings of Bhairavas and Mothers
the eight Mothers.note: Each of eight Bhairavas is ritually paired with one Mother.

the four Kumāras.note: Their refusal to produce offspring provokes Brahmā's anger.

the gods.note: Ṛgvedic poetry sometimes presents Agni as generated collectively by the gods.
The gods find Agni hidden in waters and plants and negotiate his return.
Late liturgies collectively portray the gods honoring her with joined hands.
The gods initially exclude the twins from their sacrificial session or Soma share.
The gods accept the twins after they repair Sacrifice or Cyavana enforces their claim.
Brahmā convenes and advises the gods during recurring crises.
A Vedic verse calls Brahmaṇaspati father of the gods as an exaltatory title.
Later Vedic ritual identifies Bṛhaspati as priest and chaplain of the gods.
The gods exploit Gandharva desire for Vāc to obtain Soma and recover her.
The assembled gods unsuccessfully fight the newly created guardian.
The gods petition for Kalki’s descent and praise him after he restores order.
Kūrma supports Mandara while the gods churn for nectar and restored power.
The gods’ combined energies form the great goddess Mahālakṣmī.
The gods donate weapons and gifts to Mahālakṣmī for battle.
Mahālakṣmī fights for the gods and receives their praise after victory.

the gods.myth: Manu recreates beings after the flood
the gods.note: Manu recreates the gods and other beings through ascetic power after the deluge.
The gods arrange Pūṣan’s relationship with Sūryā under the power of love.
The goddess defeats the demons who had dispossessed the gods.
The gods repeatedly follow Savitr’s effective command and ritual impulsion.

the gods.myth: The gods place Sūrya in heaven
the gods.note: Collective gods generate or establish Sūrya in the celestial realm.
Later devotional works portray assemblies of gods attending Vithoba or his devotees.
The gods console grieving Yamī and create night so time can lessen her sorrow.

the gods collectively.note: Yama drinks with the assembled gods beneath a richly leafed tree.

the gopīs.note: Jagannath's wide-eyed form expresses Kṛṣṇa's overwhelming separation from Rādhā and the gopīs.
Krishna summons the gopīs, dances with each, disappears, and returns after their lament.

the gopīs.myth: Krishna publicly favors Radhika over the other cowherd women
the gopīs.note: Krishna’s attention to Radha diminishes the other gopīs’ honor.

the hell wardens.note: Some texts make hell wardens Yama’s servants, though other accounts differ.

the holy rivers.myth: Sacred rivers fill Radha’s newly excavated pond
the holy rivers.note: The personified holy waters fill Rādhā-kuṇḍa after her companions excavate it.

the other Mahāvidyās.note: Kālī appears foremost among Satī’s ten manifestations surrounding Śiva and preventing his escape.

the other Navagraha.note: Budha jointly appears with the other eight planetary deities in ritual and art.

the other Ādityas.note: Later genealogies treat the other variably enumerated Ādityas as Mitra's siblings.

the personified faculties.note: The faculties survive one another’s departure but are uprooted when Prāṇa attempts to leave.

the sacrificial sages.myth: Sages receive Surabhi after the ocean churning
the sacrificial sages.note: The sages accept Surabhi because her milk products and ghee sustain sacrifice.

the seven seers.myth: Seven seers accompany Manu through the flood
the seven seers.note: The seven seers join Manu aboard the seed-bearing ship during the epic deluge.

the ten Pracetas.note: The ten Pracetas collectively father Daksha through Māriṣā.

the unnamed Fish.note: Manu rears and protects the small fish as it grows.

the unnamed Fish.myth: The fish saves Manu from the flood
the unnamed Fish.note: The fish warns Manu, directs his shipbuilding, and tows his vessel to safety.

Ākūti.note: Ākūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.

Āstīka.note: Āstīka is Vāsuki’s nephew, born to his sister Jaratkāru.
Āstīka ends the sacrifice threatening Vāsuki and the nāga race.

Āyu.note: Urvaśī and Purūravas are parents of Āyu, ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.

Āśuśravas.note: A medieval literary tradition names the horse Āśuśravas as Uchchaihshravas’s son.

Āḍi.note: Āḍi is Andhaka’s son and later seeks revenge against Śiva.

Āṇṭāḷ.note: Later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiology identifies Āṇṭāḷ as an incarnation of Bhūdevī.

Īśāna.note: Īśāna joins the directional gods who bless Narasimha’s Ahobilam wedding.

Śabalā.note: Later retellings rename Vasiṣṭha’s wish-yielding cow Śabalā as Kamadhenu.

Śabalāśvas.note: Daksha fathers one thousand Śabalāśvas after the Haryaśvas depart.
