Śacī.note: Airāvata carries Śacī beside Indra during the journey for a Jina’s consecration.
Śacī resists Nahuṣa and helps arrange Indra’s restoration to heaven.

Śakaṭa.note: As the infant Kṛṣṇa, Vishnu destroys the supernatural cart threat Śakaṭa.

Śakaṭāsura.note: The infant Krishna destroys the demon associated with a cart.

Śakuni.note: Some variable Purāṇic genealogical compilations list Śakuni as his son.

Śakuntalā.note: Menakā bears Śakuntalā after her union with Viśvāmitra.
Menakā arranges protection for her daughter in a celestial hermitage.

Śambara.note: Indra destroys Śambara’s resistance or strongholds in Rigvedic praise.
Kāma as Pradyumna confronts Śambara after learning counter-magic from Māyāvatī.
The grown Pradyumna defeats and kills the demon Śambara.
Śambara abducts Kāma’s infant rebirth and casts him into the sea.
As Māyāvatī, Rati evades Śambara and preserves herself through magical illusion.
Rati equips Pradyumna with magic that counters Śambara’s spells and enables his death.

Śambūka.note: Rāma beheads Śambūka for austerities forbidden by the narrative’s social order.

Śani.note: Śani, a child of Vivasvant and Chāyā, is their half-brother.
Śani and Bṛhaspati appear together as members of the Navagraha ensemble.
Śani’s dangerous gaze severs or burns the infant Gaṇeśa’s head.
Śani worships Śiva or receives a place within Śaiva cosmology.
Śukra and Śani appear jointly in Navagraha ritual and iconography.
The dominant later genealogy makes Śani the son of Sūrya and Chāyā.
Later stories portray Sūrya and Śani as antagonistic or estranged.
Śani is Yama’s half-brother through their shared solar genealogy.
Śani, child of Chāyā and the Sun, is Yamī-Yamunā’s half-brother.
Later solar genealogy makes Śani Yamuna's half-brother through Chāyā.

Śarabha.note: In Vaiṣṇava counter-narratives, Narasimha intensifies into Gandabheruṇḍa and defeats Śarabha.
Śiva as Śarabha kills or dismembers Varāha’s dangerously persistent boar manifestation.
Some Śaiva texts say Śarabha subdues Vishnu’s raging Narasiṃha manifestation.

Śaryāti.note: Śaryāti appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.

Śataparvā.note: Genealogical compilations list Śataparvā as a consort of Śukra.

Śatarūpā.note: Several accounts make Śatarūpā Brahmā's daughter or bodily creation.
Brahmā desires Śatarūpā, growing directional heads as she evades his gaze.
Later cosmology identifies Śatarūpā as the consort of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Later accounts make Śatarūpā an alternative feminine partner of the creator.
Through Prasūti, Satī is a descendant of Śatarūpā.

Śataśīrṣā.note: Modern summaries name her as Vāsuki’s consort without secure early textual support.

Śatrughna.note: Śatrughna is Rāma’s half-brother, born to Sumitrā.

Śatāgāmin.note: The Padma Purāṇa names Śatāgāmin as a son of Jatāyu.

Śatākṣī.myth: Śākambharī emits battle powers against Durgama
Śatākṣī.note: The Mahāvidyās issue from Śatākṣī-Śākambharī among numerous goddess powers.

Śaṅkhacūḍa.note: Tulasi meets, debates with, and marries Śaṅkhacūḍa, whose protection depends partly upon her fidelity.

Śaṅkhāsura.note: Later retellings and paintings substitute or equate Śaṅkhāsura with Hayagrīva.

Śibi.note: Some Purāṇic genealogical lists add Śibi as his son.

Śilpin.note: Community genealogies name Śilpin among Viśvakarman's five artisan sons.

Śiva.note: Śiva contains the poison arising in the same churning cycle as Airāvata.
Airāvata worships Śiva at Darasuram and recovers his lost white color.
Śiva turns the darkness caused by Devī into Andhaka.
Andhaka is born from Śiva’s body and placed with Hiraṇyākṣa.
Heat and sweat generated when Pārvatī covers Śiva’s eyes produce Andhaka.
The converted Andhaka acknowledges Tryambaka as his father.
Andhaka attacks Śiva and his hosts while attempting to seize Pārvatī.
Śiva wounds, impales, and purifies Andhaka after their battle.
Śiva frees Andhaka’s daitya nature, heals him, and makes him a gaṇa leader.
She is Śiva's beloved and Kāśī's co-sovereign.
She serves food to the begging Śiva from her inexhaustible kitchen.

Śiva.myth: Māyā debate and withdrawal of food
Śiva.note: She withdraws food after Śiva devalues the material world as illusion.
She defeats Śiva at dice, precipitating dispute, hunger, and eventual feeding.
After covering Śiva's eyes she darkens and must feed Kāśī to regain Gaurī form.
Apsarases attend Śiva’s processions and celebrate his acts.
Śiva develops faces in multiple directions so he can continue watching Tilottamā.
The directional guardians surround, praise and attend Śiva as subordinate cosmic powers.
The collective’s northeastern guardian Īśāna is understood as a form or emanation of Śiva.
Śiva's seed or generative power produces Ayyappa with Mohinī.
Śiva is present with Bali when the gods honor Vāmana’s authority.

Śiva.myth: Śiva manifests Bhairava from anger to punish Brahmā
Śiva.note: Śiva produces Bhairava as his punitive agent.
Some traditions treat Bhairava as Śiva himself or Śiva’s highest nature.
Śiva’s grove indirectly causes Ilā’s transformation preceding Ilā’s meeting with Budha.
Śiva contains the poison before Dhanvantari emerges bearing nectar; they do not converse.
Śiva stands as Dhanvantari’s initiatory predecessor through the mediation of Garuḍa.
Śiva’s radiance forms the warrior Goddess’s face.
Śiva gives the Goddess his trident.
She sends Śiva as her messenger, thereby receiving the title Śivadūtī.
Through identification with Pārvatī, Durgā becomes Śiva’s wife.
Gandharvas attend and sing at Śiva’s wedding, dances, battles, and epiphanies.
A Mughal manuscript illustration depicts Śiva receiving or embracing Hayagrīva.
After Hiraṇyākṣa’s austerities, Śiva gives him Andhaka to adopt.
Some epic and Purāṇic variants show Indra resisting Śiva before submitting.
Other traditions place Indra among gods seeking and receiving Śiva’s protection.
Later Puri sacred geography assigns Lokanātha Śiva as a guardian of Jagannath's field.
Tamil place-legend says Jatāyu worshipped Śiva at Vaitheeswaran Koil.

Śiva.myth: Śiva sent as the Goddess’s messenger
Śiva.note: Under a disputed identification with Śivadūtī, Kālī has Śiva deliver the Goddess’s demand.
Tantric and Bengali traditions pair Kālī and Śiva as wife and husband or Power and consciousness.
Kālī steps upon Śiva, whose contact halts or transforms her cosmic frenzy.
Some Tantras frame Śiva as teacher and Kālī or Devī as questioner.
Some Tantric systems reverse the hierarchy and present supreme Kālī as teacher.

Śiva.myth: Śiva grants Kalki three divine gifts
Śiva.note: After Kalki worships him, Śiva grants Devadatta, an irresistible sword, and Śuka.
Froth from Surabhi’s daughters touches Śiva, whose angry glance changes their colors.

Śiva.myth: Surabhi falsely confirms Brahmā reached the liṅga’s summit
Śiva.note: Surabhi supports Brahmā’s false testimony concerning Śiva’s endless fiery liṅga.

Śiva.myth: Śiva curses Surabhi for false testimony
Śiva.note: Śiva curses Surabhi or cattle after she supports Brahmā’s false claim.
Keezhperumpallam tradition says Ketu worshipped Śiva after the churning or a curse.
Krishna fights Śiva while attacking Bāṇa’s forces.
Krishna accepts Śiva’s intercession and spares the defeated Bāṇa.
Sectarian narratives say Śiva grants boons to Krishna after receiving his worship.
Śiva drinks the poison before Lakṣmī emerges from the ocean.

Śiva.myth: Satī surrounds Śiva with ten forms
Śiva.note: The Mahāvidyās block Śiva’s escape until he yields to Satī.
At Kāmarūpa, Kālī-Kāmākhyā sits upon a corpse identified as Śiva.

Śiva.myth: Kālī stands upon or unites with Śiva
Śiva.note: Kālī stands on, sexually unites with, or is paired with Śiva-Mahākāla.
At Tārāpīṭh, Tārā nurses Śiva after poison afflicts him.
Tripurasundarī is paired with Śiva in his Kāmeśvara form.
The text assigns three-eyed Śiva-Tryambaka as Bhuvaneśvarī’s partner.
Dhūmāvatī arises when Pārvatī swallows Śiva and smoke issues from her.
After emerging, Śiva requires the husband-consuming goddess to bear widowhood’s marks.
In some versions, substances associated with disguised Śiva help generate Mātaṅgī.

Śiva.myth: Creation of the Goddess from divine radiance
Śiva.note: Śiva's anger at Mahiṣa emits radiance and he gives the Goddess a trident.
South Indian variants portray Mahiṣa as Śiva's devotee, complicating his killing.

Śiva.myth: Birth from Śiva’s sweat after Satī’s death
Śiva.note: Drops of Śiva’s sweat fall upon Earth and become Mangala.
After Bhauma worships him, Śiva grants him planetary status.
Śiva grants Aṅgāraka permanent movement among the planets.
Aṅgāraka installs Śaṅkara at the tīrtha after receiving his boon.
Śiva projects Māheśvarī bearing his trident, crescent, serpents, and associated form.
Śiva delivers the ultimatum while Śivadūtī and the Mothers share Caṇḍikā’s battle company.
In Śaiva variants, Śiva creates or summons the Mothers to control Andhaka’s blood.
Fire from Śiva’s third eye burns the worlds before Matsya’s inundation.
Vāsuki adorns Śiva and sometimes forms the bowstring of his cosmic weapon.
Nandin serves as Śiva’s attendant and bars access to Kailāsa.
As chamberlain, Nandin enforces silence and protects the meditating god.
Śiva promises to become Śilāda’s son and manifests as Nandin.
Śiva makes Nandin immortal, Śiva-like, and chief of the gaṇas.
Śiva grants Nandin weapons, a garland, authority, and perpetual proximity.
Nandin transmits doctrines and practices originally revealed by Śiva.
Śiva warns the proud Nārada not to boast to Viṣṇu about defeating desire.

Śiva.myth: Planetary powers become beneficent through Śiva's presence
Śiva.note: Śiva's presence makes the nine planetary powers beneficent to his devotee.
Śaiva retellings understand Rudra's punishment of the transgressive creator as Śiva's deed.
Śiva participates in divine assemblies concerning the world's order and burden.
Śaiva theology associates Earth with one of Śiva's elemental forms.
A tīrtha legend makes Rāhu a pilgrim and worshipper of Śiva’s local liṅga.
Rāvaṇa attempts to lift Śiva's mountain, but Śiva pins him beneath it.
After Rāvaṇa's praise and penance, Śiva releases and favors him.
Rāma strings and breaks Śiva’s bow to win Sītā.
Rāma establishes or worships Śiva’s liṅga before crossing to Laṅkā.
Ravana tries to uproot Śiva’s mountain after Nandin bars his passage.
Śiva effortlessly traps Ravana’s arms beneath Kailāsa with one toe.
After Ravana praises him, Śiva releases him, names him, and grants favor.

The eleven are identified as Śiva’s manifestations, forms, followers, or emanations.
The one Rudra-Śiva assumes or emanates eleven Rudra forms.

The sages negotiate with the bride’s parents and arrange Śiva’s marriage.

Śiva.note: Śiva’s bodily rebirth of Śukra supplies an etymology for his name.

Śaiva texts identify Sūrya with, subordinate him to, or derive him from Śiva.

Śiva receives the sacred river descending from Trivikrama’s washed foot.
Śiva attends the divine gathering associated with Vāmana’s installation and victory.
Varāha burrows downward seeking Śiva’s base but cannot find the fiery pillar’s end.
Śiva participates in appropriating sacrificial aspects arising from Varāha’s destroyed body.
Some accounts include Śiva before Varuṇa in the bow’s succession of divine owners.

Śiva.myth: Poison crisis during the ocean churning
Śiva.note: Vāsuki emits poison under strain, and Śiva neutralizes the resulting catastrophe.
Later Śaiva tradition portrays Vāsuki as Śiva’s devotee and principal neck-serpent.

Śiva.myth: Forging the trident from solar radiance
Śiva.note: Viśvakarman fashions Śiva's trident from the Sun's removed brilliance.
Mahādeva supplies destructive energy that participates in Vṛtra's defeat.
Yakshas enter Śiva’s entourage through Kubera’s alliance, devotion, and neighboring rule near Kailāsa.
Śiva emerges from the liṅga and fights or subdues Yama.
Some variants say Śiva kills Yama, who is later restored so death may continue.

Śivadūtī.note: Kālī and Śivadūtī fight in the same climactic battle cycle.
She destroyed other asuras immediately before Raktabīja advanced; they never directly interacted.
Śivadūtī warns Śumbha to restore the three worlds or face destruction.

Śiva’s gaṇas.note: The guardian battles Śiva’s attendants and defeats many of them.
After restoration, Gaṇeśa is appointed lord over Śiva’s hosts.

Śiśupāla.note: Śiśupāla is identified as Jaya’s third birth after Hiranyakashipu.

Śraddhā.note: Later genealogical traditions variously name Śraddhā as Bṛhaspati’s mother.
Some epic-associated genealogies make Śraddhā Kāma’s mother through Dharma.
Several later accounts identify Śraddhā as Vaivasvata Manu’s wife or ritual partner.

Śrī.note: Originally distinct prosperity powers, Śrī and Lakṣmī were eventually canonically identified.
Sarasvatī and Śrī appear as coordinated protectors of the Dharma and polity.

Śrīdevī.note: Śrīdevī flanks Matsya as Vedanārāyaṇa, representing Viṣṇu’s consort rather than Matsya’s independent wife.

Śrīdāman.myth: Radha and Śrīdāman quarrel over Krishna and Virajā
Śrīdāman.note: Śrīdāman defends Krishna during Radha’s jealous confrontation.

Śrīdāman.myth: Radha curses Śrīdāman to be born as a demon
Śrīdāman.note: Radha’s curse causes Śrīdāman’s demonic earthly birth.

Śrīdāman.myth: Śrīdāman curses Radha to earthly birth and separation
Śrīdāman.note: His counter-curse condemns Radha to earthly life and prolonged separation.

Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha.note: Datta tradition presents Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha as Dattātreya's successive manifestation.

Śubhā.note: One epic genealogy names Śubhā as Bṛhaspati’s mother.

Śuci.note: Some Purāṇic genealogies name Śuci among Agni’s progeny.

Śuka.note: Some differing accounts make Ghṛtācī the mother of Śuka.
The omniscient parrot scouts, carries messages, and arranges Kalki’s union with Padmāvatī.

Śuṣkarevatī.note: Śuṣkarevatī consumes the remaining blood-born Andhakas without becoming sated.

Śuṣṇa.note: Indra defeats the named enemy Śuṣṇa in Rigvedic martial praise.

Śyena.note: The divine bird brings the sacred Soma to Manu.

Śyenī.note: Jatāyu belongs to the avian lineage descending from Śyenī.
The Mahābhārata genealogy names Śyenī as Sampāti’s mother.

Śāntinātha.note: Garuḍa serves as Śāntinātha's attendant yakṣa in Śvetāmbara lists.

Śīghraga.note: Later encyclopedic interpretation treats Śīghraga as another son of Sampāti.

Śūrapadma.note: Tamil tradition makes Tāraka a brother of Śūrapadma.

Śūrapadma.myth: The asura brothers wage war against Murukaṉ
Śūrapadma.note: Tāraka serves within the allied asura family and campaign headed by Śūrapadma.

Śūrpaṇakhā.note: Śūrpaṇakhā is Kubera’s paternal half-sister in the dominant genealogy.
He mocks her proposal, then cuts off her nose and ears.
Rāma rejects and ridicules Śūrpaṇakhā before Lakṣmaṇa mutilates her.
Śūrpaṇakhā is Ravana’s sister; her mutilation helps precipitate his retaliation.

Śṛgāla Vāsudeva.note: Paraśurāma directs Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma’s campaign against Śṛgāla Vāsudeva.

Ūrjasvatī.note: Genealogical compilations list Ūrjasvatī as a consort of Śukra.

ʿAlī.note: Some Ismaili and Satpanth traditions use Kalki-Nikalank language to interpret ʿAlī.

Ḍākinī.myth: Chinnamastā feeds attendants with her blood
Ḍākinī.note: One lateral blood stream from Chinnamastā’s neck feeds Ḍākinī.

Ṛbhu.note: Her silent withdrawal after his request precipitates Ṛbhu's realization of the Self.

Ṛbhus.note: The Ṛbhus remake Tvaṣṭṛ’s cup into four despite his hostility, winning divine recognition.

Ṛcīka.note: Ṛcīka is Paraśurāma’s paternal grandfather in the dominant genealogy.

Ṛddhi.note: Some differing texts name prosperity-personified Ṛddhi as Kubera’s consort.

Ṛṣabhanātha.note: Airāvata transports Indra and Indrāṇī to collect the newborn Jina.
Gomukha and Cakreśvarī are assigned as Ṛṣabhanātha’s yaksha and yakshi attendants.

Ṣaḍgarbhas.myth: Murder of Devakī’s first six sons
Ṣaḍgarbhas.note: Kamsa kills the six divine infants whose expanded prehistory reflects later theology.
